topics.name: Catalysts for change and IT milestones
Introduction to ethics: terms and rationalizations
Rule utilitarianism and limits of utilitarianism
Comparing theories and breaking the law
Networked communications: spam, crypto, trust, addiction
Censorship, free expression, and children online
Intellectual property rights, protections, and fair use
Digital media, P2P, software IP, and open source
Government databases, data mining, national ID, and dissemination
Professional ethics, the Software Engineering Code, and whistle-blowing
Globalization, the digital divide, and winner-take-all

questions.q: According to Quinn, which two developments are the main catalysts of the Information Age?
choices: The printing press and the electric telegraph
Artificial intelligence and the rise of social media platforms
Military research funding and the space race
Low-cost computers and high-speed communication networks
questions.explain: Quinn names cheap computers and fast networks as the catalysts that give the modern era its unprecedented access to information. AI and social media are products of the era, not the catalysts he identifies.

questions.q: What is the 'social-technological cycle' that serves as the theme of Chapter 1?
choices: Governments choose which technologies to adopt, and society follows them
Technology advances on its own schedule and society simply adapts afterward
Each new technology completely replaces the institutions that came before it
Social conditions lead to new technologies, and adopting them changes social conditions
questions.explain: The theme is a two-way loop: society shapes technology, and technology reshapes society. The 'technology advances on its own' option describes one-way technological determinism, which leaves out half of the cycle.

questions.q: Which company completed the UNIVAC in 1951 and delivered it to the U.S. Bureau of the Census?
choices: Bell Labs
Remington-Rand
IBM
Intel
questions.explain: Remington-Rand built UNIVAC, the first commercial computer, which also famously predicted the 1952 presidential election. IBM is the tempting answer, but it only came to dominate the mainframe market later, by the mid-1960s.

questions.q: Why did IBM come to dominate the mainframe market by the mid-1960s, even though Remington-Rand had the first commercial computer?
choices: It was the only firm legally allowed to sell to the federal government
It held the transistor patent and refused to license it to rivals
It shipped the first personal computer with a graphical interface
Bigger customer base, superior sales and marketing, and more R&D investment
questions.explain: Quinn credits IBM's customer base, sales force and R&D spending. The transistor came out of Bell Labs, not IBM, so the patent option is wrong.

questions.q: What made the IBM System/360 a milestone?
choices: It was the first machine built from IBM-invented integrated circuits
Its 19 models of varying power all ran the same programs
It was the first computer to divide its time among many terminal users
It was programmed by plugging wires into removable plugboards
questions.explain: Before System/360, IBM's computers were incompatible, and switching machines meant rewriting programs. With System/360, customers could upgrade without rewriting software. Sharing one computer through terminals describes time-sharing systems, a separate milestone.

questions.q: Where and when was the microprocessor, the 'computer on a chip' that made personal computers practical, invented?
choices: At Fairchild Semiconductor in 1958
At Intel in 1970
At Xerox PARC in 1973
At Bell Labs in 1948
questions.explain: The microprocessor was invented at Intel in 1970. Bell Labs in 1948 is when and where the transistor was invented, which makes that choice easy to mix up.

questions.q: Which programming language was a U.S. Department of Defense standard designed for business applications?
choices: Assembly language
BASIC
COBOL
FORTRAN
questions.explain: COBOL was the DoD standard for business applications. FORTRAN was the first higher-level language, but it was designed for scientific work.

questions.q: Which statement about the first U.S. telegraph line is accurate?
choices: Funded by the Pony Express, it was built coast to coast to replace riders
Funded by France, it extended the semaphore tower line from Paris to Lille
Government-funded, it was built by Samuel Morse from Washington, D.C. to Baltimore
Privately funded, it was built by Alexander Graham Bell from Boston to New York
questions.explain: Morse built the 40-mile line in 1843-1844 with government money. The transcontinental line finished in 1861 is what put Pony Express riders out of work, and the semaphore towers were a French system from 1794.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the social impacts of the telephone that Quinn lists?
choices: It blurred the line between public and private life
It increased privacy by replacing in-person visits
It ended the use of written mail for business
It made it harder for strangers to form communities
questions.explain: Quinn says the telephone blurred public and private life, eroded hierarchies, reduced privacy and enabled the first 'online' communities. Saying it increased privacy reverses what he says.

questions.q: Why was ARPANET given a decentralized, packet-switched design?
choices: To make email delivery instantaneous
To improve the network's survivability
To stay compatible with old telegraph lines
To let the government bill users per packet
questions.explain: ARPA's decentralized design meant the network could keep working if parts of it failed, and packet switching replaced circuit switching. The other options are not reasons Quinn gives.

questions.q: Who designed the TCP/IP protocol, which defines the Internet as a 'network of networks'?
choices: J. C. R. Licklider and Douglas Engelbart
Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak
Ray Tomlinson and Larry Roberts
questions.explain: Kahn conceived open-architecture networking, and Cerf and Kahn designed TCP/IP. Tomlinson and Roberts are associated with email, and Licklider imagined the 'Galactic Network'.

questions.q: How does Google's PageRank judge the importance of a Web page?
choices: By the number and quality of pages linking to it
By how often the page repeats the search keywords
By how recently the page's content was updated
By how much the page's owner pays for placement
questions.explain: PageRank looks at incoming links weighted by their quality, which is the key to Google's high precision. Keyword frequency is an older, easily gamed signal.

questions.q: A startup rents storage and computing power from Amazon Web Services and pays only for what it uses each month. Which cloud model is this?
choices: Time-sharing
Infrastructure as a service
Software as a service
Virtualization as a product
questions.explain: Paying as you go for remote storage and computation is infrastructure as a service. Software as a service delivers finished applications, such as Microsoft Office 365.

questions.q: In Quinn's terminology, which term means 'the rational examination of morality'?
choices: Morality
Society
Ethics
Rationalization
questions.explain: Ethics is the rational, systematic evaluation of morality and behavior. Morality is a society's rules of conduct, the thing ethics examines.

questions.q: In Quinn's terms, what is 'morality'?
choices: A society's rules about what people ought and ought not to do
An individual's private feelings about right and wrong
The rational study of why people behave as they do
The set of statutes passed by a legislature
questions.explain: Morality is the set of rules of conduct, and ethics is the rational examination of those rules. Morality is broader than written law.

questions.q: Which three 'core values' does Quinn say nearly everyone shares?
choices: Liberty, equality, and fraternity
Wealth, fame, and power
Life, happiness, and agency
Honesty, courage, and generosity
questions.explain: Quinn lists life, happiness and agency (the ability to accomplish goals). Honesty, courage and generosity are virtues from virtue ethics, not the core values he describes.

questions.q: What separates the ethical point of view from the selfish point of view?
choices: It always puts others' interests ahead of your own
It relies on guidance from religious authority
It respects other people's core values, not only your own
It considers only the consequences of actions
questions.explain: Taking the ethical point of view means giving weight to other people's core values. It does not demand total self-sacrifice, which is the trap in the 'always puts others ahead' option.

questions.q: What is a rationalization, and why do people use them?
choices: A cost-benefit estimate, used to compare alternative actions
A logical proof that an act is right, used to persuade others
A universalized rule, used to test whether an act is permissible
A moral excuse for an immoral act, used to protect one's self-image
questions.explain: Quinn calls a rationalization a justification for an immoral action that protects our self-image. Rationalizations short-circuit ethical thinking rather than making it rigorous.

questions.q: According to Quinn, what is wrong with rationalizations?
choices: They are always built on claims that are factually false
They short-circuit ethical thinking about duties, rights and consequences
They focus too heavily on distant, long-term consequences
They are available only to people holding positions of authority
questions.explain: The problem is that rationalizations stop real ethical analysis: we forget our duties, others' rights, the consequences, and what a virtuous person would do. They are not necessarily factually false, which is why they can be so persuasive.

questions.q: An engineer says, 'If I refuse to ship this unsafe code, my manager will just get someone else to do it.' What is this?
choices: An exercise of a negative right
An application of the categorical imperative
A rule utilitarian calculation
A rationalization
questions.explain: 'There's no point losing my job, they'll just bring in someone else' is one of the rationalizations on Quinn's list. It excuses the act instead of evaluating it.

questions.q: Which statement is one of the rationalizations Quinn lists?
choices: I would not want someone to do this to me, so I won't
A person of good character would not act this way
If everyone did this, the practice would defeat itself
It will hurt them, but they are bad people who deserve it
questions.explain: Calling the victims bad people who deserve it is on Quinn's list. The other three are legitimate ethical reasoning: a role-reversal check, universalization, and a virtue test.

questions.q: What makes an ethical theory 'workable' in Quinn's sense?
choices: Its conclusions match the majority opinion in a society
Its conclusions always match what the law requires
It is endorsed by a recognized religious authority
Its explanations could persuade a skeptical yet open-minded audience
questions.explain: Quinn wants conclusions supported by facts, shared values and logic that a skeptical but open-minded listener could accept. Majority opinion alone is the cultural relativist standard he rejects.

questions.q: In the Alexis scenario, she uses a stolen login to get into a private college's computers. One discussion question asks, 'Would you call Alexis a good role model for other students?' Which theory does that question reflect most directly?
choices: Virtue ethics
Act utilitarianism
Divine command theory
Social contract theory
questions.explain: Asking whether someone is a good role model looks at character, which is what virtue ethics cares about. The questions about who benefited and who was harmed are the ones that line up with utilitarianism.

questions.q: According to Quinn, why do communities exist even though they impose costs, such as prohibited and obligatory actions?
choices: A divine authority commands people to live together
Their benefits, such as security and trade, outweigh the costs
Nobody can physically survive in complete isolation
People are legally forced to join one at birth
questions.explain: Quinn presents community life as a trade-off in which the benefits win. The other options bring in coercion or religious claims that are not part of his account.

questions.q: What is the central claim of ethical relativism?
choices: There are no universal standards of right and wrong
Moral rules are valid only if all could follow them
Right and wrong are fixed by God's will
An act is right if it maximizes total happiness
questions.explain: Relativism denies universal moral standards, so two people can disagree about an action and both be correct. The 'all could follow them' option describes Kant's universalizability test, an objectivist idea.

questions.q: Which slogan best captures subjective relativism?
choices: What's right for you may not be right for me
The greatest happiness for the greatest number
When in Rome, do as the Romans do
Do unto others as you would have them do unto you
questions.explain: Subjective relativism says each person decides right and wrong for themselves. 'When in Rome' fits cultural relativism, where society rather than the individual sets the standard.

questions.q: Which of these does Quinn use as an argument against subjective relativism?
choices: It cannot resolve conflicts between two perfect duties
It requires too many calculations of costs and benefits
Nobody ever actually signed a contract agreeing to it
It blurs doing what you think is right with doing what you feel like
questions.explain: Quinn says subjective relativism makes it easy to rationalize. The other choices are his criticisms of utilitarianism, Kantianism and social contract theory.

questions.q: How does Quinn respond to the idea that subjective relativism is just a form of tolerance?
choices: Tolerance applies only to cultures, not to individuals
Subjective relativism and tolerance are two different things
Tolerance requires subjective relativism, so it is workable
Tolerance is a vice, so subjective relativism is wrong
questions.explain: Quinn separates the two. A subjective relativist has no grounds to call tolerance universally good, since an intolerant person would be 'right for themselves' too.

questions.q: What does cultural relativism hold?
choices: Right and wrong are what rational people would agree to
Right and wrong depend on a society's actual moral guidelines
Right and wrong depend on each individual's feelings
Right and wrong are set by a culture's holy books
questions.explain: Cultural relativism ties morality to a society's actual norms, which vary from place to place and over time. 'What rational people would agree to' is social contract theory, which justifies rules by reason rather than custom.

questions.q: Which argument is part of Quinn's 'case for' cultural relativism?
choices: It treats all persons as moral equals
We owe obedience to our Creator
Ethical debates are pointless
It is arrogant for one society to judge another
questions.explain: The case for cultural relativism is that different contexts need different rules and that judging other societies is arrogant. 'Ethical debates are pointless' belongs to the case for subjective relativism.

questions.q: Quinn says 'Because two societies have different moral views doesn't mean they ought to have different views.' What weakness of cultural relativism does this point to?
choices: It moves from what norms are to what they should be
It relies on predicting uncertain consequences
It makes ethical theories too hard to apply
It ignores the role of emotions in moral life
questions.explain: That something is the case does not show it ought to be. The other options are criticisms of other theories.

questions.q: What is the 'many/any fallacy' that Quinn raises against cultural relativism?
choices: Inferring that any practice is acceptable because many are
Inferring that a rule needs many exceptions to be valid
Inferring that any popular rule produces happiness
Inferring that a belief is true because many hold it
questions.explain: Admitting that many different practices can be acceptable does not mean every practice is. 'Many people believe it, so it's true' is a different fallacy, the appeal to popularity.

questions.q: A student says, 'Downloading pirated movies is wrong for you if you believe it's wrong, but it's fine for me because I don't.' Which view is this?
choices: Subjective relativism
Cultural relativism
Ethical egoism
Act utilitarianism
questions.explain: Each individual deciding right and wrong for themselves is subjective relativism. If the student had appealed to the norms of their society, it would be cultural relativism.

questions.q: A manager argues, 'Paying bribes to officials is normal in that country, so it's morally right for us to pay them when we do business there.' Which view is the manager using?
choices: Cultural relativism
Rule utilitarianism
Divine command theory
Subjective relativism
questions.explain: The manager makes rightness depend on the host society's actual norms. That is cultural relativism, not a personal judgment of the kind subjective relativism relies on.

questions.q: A critic says that under cultural relativism, the reformers who first spoke out against slavery in their own society were wrong simply because they went against its norms. Which of Quinn's objections is the critic making?
choices: It doesn't account for the evolution of moral guidelines
Societies do, in fact, share certain core values
It provides no way out for cultures in conflict
It fails when a society has no cultural norms
questions.explain: If the current norms define what's right, moral reformers are always wrong, so the theory cannot explain moral progress. 'No way out for cultures in conflict' is a separate objection about clashes between societies.

questions.q: What is Quinn's final verdict on subjective relativism and cultural relativism?
choices: Both are workable ethical theories
Neither is a workable ethical theory
Only cultural relativism is workable
Only subjective relativism is workable
questions.explain: Quinn rejects both. Subjective relativism lets decisions rest on something other than reason, and cultural relativism is based on reason only indirectly.

questions.q: Under divine command theory, what makes an action good?
choices: It serves the agent's long-term interest
It maximizes total happiness
It is what a virtuous person would do
It is aligned with God's will
questions.explain: Good actions are those aligned with God's will, and bad actions go against it. The other options are utilitarianism, virtue ethics and egoism.

questions.q: According to divine command theory, how do we learn God's will?
choices: Through calculating each action's consequences
Through each person's private feelings
Through holy books, used as moral guides
Through laws passed by elected legislatures
questions.explain: The theory treats holy books as revealing God's will. Private feelings would be a subjective relativist source.

questions.q: Which of these is an argument in Quinn's 'case for' divine command theory?
choices: Its rules can be tested by universalizing them
It is the only theory grounded purely in reason
Different holy books agree on every important teaching
God is all-good, all-knowing, and the ultimate authority
questions.explain: Supporters say we owe obedience to our Creator, who is all-good, all-knowing and the ultimate authority. The claim that holy books all agree is false, and its opposite is one of Quinn's objections.

questions.q: Why does Quinn call divine command theory impractical for analyzing moral problems in a society like the United States?
choices: Holy books are too difficult to translate accurately
Most moral questions are already settled by existing law
Society is multicultural and secular, without one shared religious authority
Religious believers never disagree among themselves
questions.explain: Arguments that depend on one faith's scripture will not persuade people of other faiths or of none. That is why Quinn says the theory is not workable 'for our purposes'.

questions.q: A software developer tries to decide whether it is moral to scrape users' public posts to train a machine-learning model by searching a holy text for guidance. Which of Quinn's objections to divine command theory fits best?
choices: It is based on obedience rather than reason
Some modern moral problems are not directly addressed in scripture
Different holy books disagree on certain teachings
No one ever actually signed the social contract
questions.explain: Ancient texts do not speak directly to data scraping or machine learning, so the theory gives no direct guidance. Disagreement between holy books is a real objection but not the one this scenario shows.

questions.q: Quinn says divine command theory is 'based on obedience, not reason.' Why does this matter for his project?
choices: Virtue ethics classifies obedience as a vice
Obedience to any authority always leads to bad outcomes
His approach requires conclusions reasoned from facts and shared values
Reason and religion are always in direct conflict
questions.explain: A workable theory has to persuade a skeptical audience through reason. Quinn does not claim obedience always produces bad outcomes.

questions.q: Two members of a corporate ethics committee belong to different religions, and their scriptures give conflicting guidance on a workplace issue. Which weakness of divine command theory does this show?
choices: The theory ignores consequences entirely
The theory cannot guide government policy
The theory commits the many/any fallacy
Different holy books disagree on certain teachings
questions.explain: When scriptures conflict, divine command theory cannot settle which divine will to follow. 'Cannot guide government policy' is one of Quinn's objections to virtue ethics.

questions.q: Where does divine command theory fall on the objectivism versus relativism spectrum?
choices: Neither, since it rests on revelation rather than reason
Subjective relativism, since faith is a personal matter
Relativism, since morality varies from one religion to another
Objectivism, since morality exists outside the human mind
questions.explain: Quinn lists divine command theory among the objectivist theories, since moral truth comes from God rather than human invention. The variety of religions is a practical problem for the theory, not a reason to call it relativist.

questions.q: What is Quinn's conclusion about divine command theory?
choices: It is workable but less practical than Kantianism
It is workable only when combined with utilitarianism
It is not a workable ethical theory for our purposes
It is the most workable theory because of its authority
questions.explain: Quinn concludes it is not workable for his purposes, mainly because it rests on obedience and on religious authority that people do not share.

questions.q: Someone argues, 'Stealing is wrong simply because God forbids it, and no further reason is needed.' Which theory is this?
choices: Kantianism
Social contract theory
Divine command theory
Cultural relativism
questions.explain: Making an action's wrongness depend entirely on God's prohibition is divine command theory. A Kantian would argue that the rule fails universalization or uses people as mere means.

questions.q: According to ethical egoism, what is the morally right action?
choices: The one required by duty regardless of results
The one maximizing happiness for everyone affected
The one giving oneself the maximum long-term benefit
The one a person feels like doing at the moment
questions.explain: Ethical egoism says each person should focus exclusively on their own long-term self-interest. It concerns long-term benefit, not momentary desire.

questions.q: Which author does Quinn mention as having espoused a theory similar to ethical egoism, while noting that his section is not a summary of her theory?
choices: Ayn Rand
Mary Wollstonecraft
Judith Jarvis Thomson
Hannah Arendt
questions.explain: Ayn Rand, author of The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged, held a view similar to egoism. Judith Jarvis Thomson comes up later, in the privacy chapter.

questions.q: Which argument does Quinn include among the reasons offered in favor of ethical egoism?
choices: It treats every person as a moral equal
It respects the ethical point of view
It distributes benefits in a just way
It is practical, since we already favor ourselves
questions.explain: Supporters say egoism is practical, that others can take care of themselves, that the community benefits, and that other moral principles grow out of self-interest. By definition it does not take the ethical point of view.

questions.q: To the claim that egoism is good because it is practical, Quinn replies:
choices: People who consider others lead happier lives
Self-interest can lead to blatantly immoral behavior
An easy moral philosophy may not be the best moral philosophy
We know a lot about what is good for someone else
questions.explain: Being easy to follow does not make a theory correct. 'We know a lot about what is good for someone else' answers a different pro-egoism argument, that we should let others take care of themselves.

questions.q: Which pro-egoism argument does Quinn's point 'We know a lot about what is good for someone else' answer?
choices: The community benefits when individuals put themselves first
It is better to let other people take care of themselves
We are already inclined to do what is best for ourselves
Other moral principles are rooted in self-interest
questions.explain: Egoists say we don't know what's good for others, so we should leave them alone. Quinn replies that we often do know, for example that people need food and medical care.

questions.q: A software consultant could secretly bill a client for hours she never worked and would almost certainly not be caught. An egoist reasons that the extra money serves her interest, so padding the bill is right. Which of Quinn's criticisms does this show?
choices: An easy moral philosophy may not be the best
Self-interest can lead to blatantly immoral behavior
There is no way to resolve conflicts between perfect duties
It is unclear how far into the future to calculate
questions.explain: When doing wrong pays and is undetectable, egoism can endorse it. That is Quinn's point that self-interest can justify blatantly immoral acts.

questions.q: A shop owner never cheats customers. She reasons that a reputation for honesty brings repeat business and is best for her over the long run. Her reasoning best fits which theory?
choices: Kantianism
Ethical egoism
Act utilitarianism
Virtue ethics
questions.explain: She is honest because it maximizes her own long-term benefit, which is the egoist test. A Kantian would be honest out of duty whatever the payoff.

questions.q: An egoist argues, 'When each person pursues their own profit, the whole economy grows and everyone ends up better off.' Which pro-egoism argument is this?
choices: The community can benefit when individuals put their well-being first
It is better to let others take care of themselves
It is practical because we already act this way
Other moral principles are rooted in self-interest
questions.explain: This is the claim that self-interest produces collective benefit. The 'rooted in self-interest' argument says something different: that duties like honesty exist only because they serve us.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say ethical egoism fails at the most basic level?
choices: It requires people to sacrifice their own happiness
It depends entirely on religious authority
By definition, it ignores the ethical point of view
It weighs consequences instead of duties
questions.explain: The ethical point of view requires respecting other people's core values, and egoism tells you to focus only on your own. Egoism does consider consequences, but only to yourself.

questions.q: What is Quinn's overall verdict on ethical egoism?
choices: It is the most practical workable theory
It is not a workable ethical theory
It is workable if combined with virtue ethics
It is workable only for business decisions
questions.explain: Quinn concludes ethical egoism is not workable. He also notes that people who take the good of others into account tend to lead happier lives.

questions.q: According to Kant, what is the only thing in the world that is good without qualification?
choices: A good will
Happiness
Knowledge
Courage
questions.explain: Kant held that only a good will, the desire to do the right thing, is good without qualification. Happiness or courage can serve bad ends, which is why they need qualification.

questions.q: Which statement is the first formulation of the categorical imperative?
choices: Treat yourself and others as ends, never only as means
Act only from moral rules you can will to be universal laws
Act as a virtuous person would act in your place
Act so as to produce the greatest total happiness
questions.explain: The first formulation is about universalizing your rule. The 'ends, never only as means' wording is the second formulation.

questions.q: Which formulation of the categorical imperative does Quinn say is usually easier to work with?
choices: The rule of perfect duties
The second (treat people as ends)
The first (universalize your rule)
The principle of utility
questions.explain: Quinn notes that the second formulation, treating people as ends and never only as means, is usually easier to apply. The principle of utility comes from utilitarianism, not Kant.

questions.q: A person in financial trouble considers borrowing money with a promise to repay that they don't intend to keep. Imagining a world where everyone makes promises intending to break them, they see that nobody would believe promises, so their own false promise would fail. Which reasoning is this?
choices: Act utilitarianism
The second formulation of the categorical imperative
Social contract theory
The first formulation of the categorical imperative
questions.explain: Universalizing the rule makes it defeat itself, which is the first-formulation test. A second-formulation argument would focus on using the lender as a mere means.

questions.q: Rosa buys a term paper and submits it as her own. An analysis says she deceived her professor and manipulated him to reach her goal of passing the course. Which reasoning is this?
choices: The first formulation of the categorical imperative
Rule utilitarianism
The second formulation of the categorical imperative
Virtue ethics
questions.explain: Treating the professor as a means to her end of passing is the second formulation. The first-formulation version universalizes 'you may claim credit for others' work' and shows that reports would stop being credible.

questions.q: In the Rosa case, the rule 'You may claim credit for work performed by someone else' is universalized. What does Quinn conclude?
choices: Everyone would be happier with more free time, so the rule is fine
The rule is acceptable because Rosa had a good reason
Reports would stop showing what students know, so the rule defeats itself
Professors would be justified in failing every student
questions.explain: If the rule were universal, professors would stop giving credit for reports, so the rule destroys the practice it relies on. Kant rejects the idea that Rosa's sympathetic situation creates an exception.

questions.q: What is Quinn's 'quick check' for whether an action may violate the categorical imperative?
choices: Add up the benefits and harms to everyone affected
Ask what most people in your society would do
Ask whether the action is permitted by law
Reverse roles: how would you react if it were done to you?
questions.explain: If you would react negatively when the roles are reversed, that suggests you are privileging yourself, which is evidence of a violation. Adding up benefits and harms is utilitarian reasoning.

questions.q: How does Kant distinguish a perfect duty from an imperfect duty?
choices: A perfect duty allows no exceptions; an imperfect duty holds only in general
A perfect duty is written in law; an imperfect duty is only a custom
A perfect duty yields the best results; an imperfect one yields mixed results
A perfect duty is owed to oneself; an imperfect duty is owed to others
questions.explain: Quinn's examples are truth-telling as a perfect duty and helping others as an imperfect duty. The distinction is about exceptions, not about who the duty is owed to.

questions.q: A programmer has promised a client to report test results truthfully and also wants to help a struggling friend by quietly shading the numbers. Under Kantianism, how is this conflict resolved?
choices: Neither duty applies, so the choice is free
Whichever choice maximizes happiness prevails
The imperfect duty of helping a friend prevails
The perfect duty of truthfulness prevails
questions.explain: When a perfect duty (truthfulness) and an imperfect duty (helping others) conflict, the perfect duty prevails. Choosing whatever maximizes happiness would be act utilitarian reasoning.

questions.q: What does Quinn identify as a key weakness of Kantianism?
choices: Conflicts between two perfect duties have no solution
It requires predicting consequences with certainty
It rests on obedience to authority rather than reason
It cannot explain why people need any privacy
questions.explain: Quinn's objections are that sometimes no rule fits an action and that rule conflicts, especially between two perfect duties, cannot be resolved, because Kantianism allows no exceptions to perfect duties. Uncertain consequences are a problem for utilitarianism.

questions.q: Which argument appears in Quinn's case for Kantianism?
choices: It treats all persons as moral equals
It recognizes the role of emotions in morality
It is down-to-earth and focuses on happiness
It is framed in the language of rights
questions.explain: Kantianism gives everyone moral worth as rational, autonomous beings, holds everyone to the same standard and produces universal guidelines. 'Down-to-earth and focused on happiness' describes act utilitarianism, and 'framed in rights' describes social contract theory.

questions.q: What is Quinn's overall verdict on Kantianism?
choices: It is workable only combined with virtue ethics
It is unworkable because it ignores consequences
It is the only workable ethical theory
Despite weaknesses, it is a workable ethical theory
questions.explain: Quinn lists Kantianism as workable along with act and rule utilitarianism, social contract theory and virtue ethics.

questions.q: The essay 'Algorithmic Exploitation and Human Dignity' tests the rule 'It is fine to manipulate users' attention to maximize engagement and profit' and argues that if every platform did this, trust and honest communication would collapse. Which part of Kant's theory is the essay using?
choices: The second formulation (ends, not means)
The first formulation (universalizability)
The Greatest Happiness Principle
The perfect/imperfect duty distinction
questions.explain: The argument universalizes the rule and finds that it destroys the system it depends on, which is the first formulation. The essay's separate second argument, about users being treated as tools, is the one that uses the second formulation.

questions.q: The same essay argues that platforms use dopamine-driven feedback loops to bypass users' conscious judgment for profit, so they turn people into instruments rather than autonomous agents. Which formulation does this argument rely on?
choices: Rawls's difference principle for social inequalities
The second formulation (treat humanity as an end, never merely as a means)
The first formulation (act only on universalizable rules)
Bentham's calculus of weighing pleasure and pain
questions.explain: Treating users as tools for profit is a second-formulation violation. The essay adds that undermining users' ability to decide freely and rationally strikes at the autonomy Kant's ethics depends on.

questions.q: Which two philosophers does Quinn associate with the principle of utility?
choices: Immanuel Kant and Aristotle
John Locke and John Rawls
Thomas Hobbes and Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
questions.explain: Bentham and Mill developed utilitarianism. Hobbes and Rousseau are social contract theorists.

questions.q: How does utilitarianism define 'utility'?
choices: The usefulness of an object for completing a practical task
The market value of a good or service to its buyers
The degree to which an action conforms to moral duty
The tendency of an object to produce happiness or prevent unhappiness
questions.explain: Utility in this sense is about producing happiness and preventing unhappiness, for an individual or a community. It is not everyday 'usefulness' or market price.

questions.q: What does the Greatest Happiness Principle state?
choices: An act is right if it benefits the least-advantaged members of society
An act is right if it benefits the greatest number, however the good is shared
An act is right to the extent it increases the affected parties' total happiness
An act is right if the agent could will it as a universal law
questions.explain: The principle is about the total happiness of everyone affected, and an act is wrong to the extent it decreases that total. Quinn warns that utilitarianism does not mean 'the greatest good of the greatest number', since that requires an added principle of justice.

questions.q: Why is utilitarianism called a consequentialist theory?
choices: It judges acts by whether they follow established rules
An act's morality depends on its consequences, not intent
It considers only consequences for the person acting
It weighs intent and consequences equally
questions.explain: For a utilitarian, the morality of an action has nothing to do with intent. Considering only the consequences for yourself would be ethical egoism.

questions.q: In weighing a pleasure, an analyst asks how soon it will arrive: next week, or a year from now. Which of Bentham's factors is this?
choices: Propinquity
Fecundity
Purity
Extent
questions.explain: Propinquity is nearness in time. Fecundity is the chance of being followed by more pleasure, purity is the chance of being free of pain, and extent is the number of people affected.

questions.q: An analyst asks how many people will feel the effects of a pleasure or pain. Which of Bentham's factors is this?
choices: Extent
Certainty
Duration
Intensity
questions.explain: Extent is the number of people affected. Intensity is how strong the experience is, and duration is how long it lasts.

questions.q: A state considers replacing a curvy highway. The costs are $20 million to compensate homeowners, $10 million in construction and $1 million in lost wildlife habitat. The benefits are $39 million in reduced driving costs. What does an act utilitarian conclude?
choices: It is wrong: removing 150 homes violates property rights
No verdict is possible without the homeowners' consent
It is wrong: wildlife habitat cannot be priced in dollars
It is good: $39M in benefits exceed $31M in costs
questions.explain: The act utilitarian adds up the costs ($31M) and benefits ($39M) and approves the project. The property-rights objection comes from social contract reasoning, not act utilitarianism.

questions.q: Which is part of Quinn's 'case for' act utilitarianism?
choices: It is framed in the language of rights
It avoids the problem of moral luck entirely
It treats all people as ends in themselves
It is practical, comprehensive, and focused on happiness
questions.explain: Quinn praises act utilitarianism for its focus on happiness, its down-to-earth practicality and its comprehensiveness. Avoiding moral luck is an advantage of rule utilitarianism.

questions.q: You send flowers to a friend in the hospital. Unknown to you, she is severely allergic and has a reaction. Under act utilitarianism your action now counts as wrong. Which criticism of act utilitarianism does this show?
choices: It is susceptible to the problem of moral luck
It offers no way out for cultures in conflict
It measures all consequences on one scale
It ignores our innate sense of duty
questions.explain: Consequences you could not foresee decide whether your act was right. That is moral luck.

questions.q: Breaking a promise to a coworker would produce slightly more total happiness than keeping it, so an act utilitarian concludes the promise should be broken. Which of Quinn's criticisms does this show?
choices: It is simply too much work
It is based on obedience, not reason
It ignores our innate sense of duty
It cannot guide government policy
questions.explain: Act utilitarianism gives promises no weight of their own, which conflicts with our sense that we have duties. 'Too much work' is a separate criticism, about how much calculation the theory demands.

questions.q: Which problem does Quinn raise specifically against act utilitarianism?
choices: It is unclear whom to include and how far ahead to look
It undermines attempts to hold people responsible
It gives no guidance when two perfect duties conflict
It assumes everyone has signed a social contract
questions.explain: Where to draw the boundaries of the calculation is a core difficulty. Other criticisms include the amount of work, ignoring duty, uncertain consequences and moral luck.

questions.q: A penniless, bedridden friend would enjoy a copy of a CD you own. Copying it gives the friend $15 of benefit and you $10 of satisfaction, and there is no lost sale and no police involvement. How does an act utilitarian judge illegally copying the CD?
choices: Wrong, because widespread copying would erode respect for law
Good, because $25 of benefit outweighs $0 of harm
Neutral, because no money actually changed hands
Wrong, because breaking the law is never justified
questions.explain: Quinn uses this example to show that act utilitarianism can approve of breaking the law. The 'widespread copying' reasoning is the rule utilitarian analysis, which reaches the opposite verdict.

questions.q: What does rule utilitarianism hold?
choices: Follow rules rational people would accept for mutual benefit
Perform whichever single act maximizes total happiness
Adopt rules that would maximize total happiness if everyone followed them
Follow rules that can be universalized without contradiction
questions.explain: Rule utilitarianism applies the principle of utility to rules rather than to individual acts. 'Rational people would accept' is social contract theory, and 'universalized without contradiction' is Kantianism.

questions.q: What is the key difference between act and rule utilitarianism?
choices: Act is concerned with rights; rule is concerned with duties
Act applies utility to individual actions; rule applies it to moral rules
Rule ignores happiness entirely and focuses on fairness
Act weighs the agent's intent; rule weighs only the consequences
questions.explain: Both are consequentialist and both care about happiness. They differ in what gets evaluated: single acts or general rules.

questions.q: In Quinn's anti-worm scenario, which worm appeared after the Blaster worm in August 2003, deleted Blaster, and downloaded a patch?
choices: The Morris Internet worm
Stuxnet
Firesheep
Nachi
questions.explain: Nachi took control of vulnerable machines, removed Blaster, installed a patch and used each computer to spread further. Firesheep was a Firefox extension, not a worm.

questions.q: Evaluate this rule: 'If I can write a helpful worm that removes a harmful worm and protects computers from future attacks, I should release it.' What does Quinn's rule utilitarian analysis conclude?
choices: Right: people who never update their systems are protected
Undecidable without knowing who wrote the worm
Right: the author's intentions are clearly good
Wrong: harms to network users and administrators outweigh the benefits
questions.explain: The harms fall on network users, system administrators and people whose computers are invaded by buggy anti-worms, and Quinn concludes they outweigh the benefits. Good intent is irrelevant to a consequentialist.

questions.q: Which of these is an advantage of rule utilitarianism over act utilitarianism, according to Quinn?
choices: It avoids moral luck and reduces bias
It has no need for a principle of justice
It never requires measuring consequences
It gives perfect duties absolute priority
questions.explain: Because rules are judged by their general consequences, one unlucky outcome does not change the verdict, and rules are harder to bend in your own favor. It still measures consequences, just for rules.

questions.q: Which statement reflects Quinn's 'case for' rule utilitarianism?
choices: It focuses on virtues rather than on consequences
Not every decision needs a fresh utilitarian calculation
It requires no agreement among members of society
Every decision gets its own complete cost-benefit tally
questions.explain: Once a good rule is established, you can follow it without recalculating, and moral rules survive exceptional situations. A fresh calculation for every decision is the act utilitarian approach.

questions.q: Which criticism does Quinn make of utilitarianism in general, both act and rule?
choices: It cannot explain why communities form
It treats people only as means to an end
It is grounded in obedience to authority
All consequences must be measured on a single scale
questions.explain: Adding up benefits and harms requires common units, which can mean putting a value on a human life. The 'means to an end' wording comes from Kant's second formulation.

questions.q: A policy would greatly increase total happiness by benefiting a large majority while imposing severe, concentrated harm on a small minority. Which criticism of utilitarianism does this show?
choices: It ignores unjust distributions of good consequences
It makes ethical debates pointless
It is based on obedience rather than reason
It cannot resolve conflicts between perfect duties
questions.explain: Utilitarianism looks at the total, not at how benefits and harms are spread. Quinn says fixing this requires a separate principle of justice.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say utilitarianism does not mean 'the greatest good of the greatest number'?
choices: That phrase requires a principle of justice in addition to utility
Utilitarians care only about the agent's own good
That phrase actually describes Kant's categorical imperative
Utilitarians refuse to count the number of people affected
questions.explain: Utilitarianism maximizes total happiness. Spreading good across the greatest number is a distribution concern, which needs a justice principle that can conflict with utility.

questions.q: A manager asks, 'What would happen if every employee in this company always reported security flaws they discovered?' and judges the policy by whether the total benefits of everyone doing so exceed the total harms. Which theory is the manager using?
choices: Act utilitarianism
Virtue ethics
Kantianism
Rule utilitarianism
questions.explain: Imagining everyone following a rule and weighing the resulting happiness is rule utilitarianism. Kant also imagines everyone following a rule, but he looks for a logical contradiction, not a balance of benefits and harms.

questions.q: What is Quinn's verdict on act and rule utilitarianism?
choices: Despite weaknesses, both are workable
Neither is workable, since both ignore justice
Only act utilitarianism is workable
Only rule utilitarianism is workable
questions.explain: Quinn lists both as workable despite the problems with measuring consequences and with justice.

questions.q: Which philosopher described life in a 'state of nature' as 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short'?
choices: John Locke
Jean-Jacques Rousseau
John Rawls
Thomas Hobbes
questions.explain: Hobbes argued that we implicitly accept a social contract, with moral rules and a government to enforce them, to escape the state of nature. Rousseau emphasized that in an ideal society no one is above the rules.

questions.q: What did Rousseau stress about the ideal society?
choices: Rules should bend to each person's preferences
A strong monarch must enforce every rule
Only property owners should write the rules
No one is above the rules, which discourages bad rules
questions.explain: Rousseau held that if everyone is bound by the rules, lawmakers have a reason not to make bad ones. Hobbes is the one who emphasized a government strong enough to enforce the rules.

questions.q: Whose definition of morality is this: 'the set of rules, governing how people are to treat one another, that rational people will agree to accept, for their mutual benefit, on the condition that others follow those rules as well'?
choices: John Stuart Mill
Immanuel Kant
Aristotle
James Rachels
questions.explain: Quinn uses James Rachels's definition to sum up social contract theory.

questions.q: Your right not to have the government censor your blog can be honored if others simply leave you alone. What kind of right is it?
choices: A positive right
An imperfect duty
A purely prudential right
A negative right
questions.explain: A negative right is one others can guarantee by leaving you alone. A positive right obliges others to do something for you.

questions.q: A right to receive a free public education obliges others to provide something on your behalf. What kind of right is it?
choices: A negative right
An absolute right
A positive right
A natural property right
questions.explain: Positive rights require action from others. Quinn notes that positive rights tend to be more limited, while negative rights tend to be more absolute.

questions.q: What correlation between types of rights does Quinn describe?
choices: Negative rights are recognized only by social contract theory
All rights tend to be equally absolute in every circumstance
Positive rights tend to be limited; negative rights tend to be absolute
Positive rights tend to be absolute; negative rights tend to be limited
questions.explain: Because positive rights demand resources and effort from others, they are usually restricted by circumstances. Negative rights cost others little, so they tend to be closer to absolute.

questions.q: Under John Rawls's principles of justice, social and economic inequalities must be tied to positions everyone has a fair and equal chance to achieve, and must also:
choices: Be approved by a majority of citizens in a vote
Most benefit the least-advantaged members of society
Reflect each person's contribution to the economy
Maximize the total happiness of all members of society
questions.explain: The second requirement is the difference principle. Maximizing total happiness is utilitarianism, not Rawls.

questions.q: A company proposes a bonus structure that gives executives much higher pay only if it also produces the largest possible improvement in the wages of its lowest-paid workers. Which principle is the company following?
choices: Bentham's principle of utility
Hobbes's state of nature
Rawls's difference principle
Kant's first formulation
questions.explain: An inequality justified by its benefit to the least-advantaged is the difference principle.

questions.q: Hao builds customer profiles from purchases at his convenience stores and sells them to direct marketers. According to Quinn's social contract analysis, what does the rightness of his action depend on?
choices: Whether a virtuous store owner would choose to sell the data
Who has rights to the transaction data, and whether confidentiality was owed
Whether Hao's underlying motives for selling were good ones
Whether marketers' gains outweigh customers' annoyance at junk mail
questions.explain: The social contract analysis is framed in terms of rights. If Hao and the customer have equal rights to the information, selling it is fine; if customers can expect confidentiality, Hao needed their permission. Weighing gains against annoyance would be utilitarian.

questions.q: Which advantage of social contract theory does the 'tragedy of the commons' illustrate?
choices: It shows how virtues develop through repeated habit
It shows why perfect duties override imperfect ones
It explains self-interested behavior when no agreement exists
It proves that self-interest always helps the community
questions.explain: Without agreed rules, each person overuses the shared resource. Social contract theory explains why we need binding agreements. The last option is an egoist claim, and the tragedy of the commons actually counts against it.

questions.q: Which weakness of social contract theory does Quinn point out?
choices: It allows no exceptions to perfect duties
It ignores the language of rights altogether
It requires calculating consequences far into the future
It may treat unjustly those unable to uphold the contract
questions.explain: Other criticisms are that no one actually signed the contract, that some actions can be described in more than one way, and that rights can conflict. The theory is framed in rights, so the last option gets it backwards.

questions.q: According to social contract theory, what is our obligation to obey the law?
choices: An obligation only when obeying maximizes happiness
No obligation, since no one actually signed the contract
A prima facie obligation, overridden only by a higher moral duty
An absolute obligation that admits no exceptions at all
questions.explain: Everyone bears burdens in exchange for benefits, so other things being equal we should obey, unless a higher-order moral obligation compels us to break the law. Obeying only when it maximizes happiness is act utilitarian reasoning.

questions.q: Which ancient traditions does Quinn identify as roots of virtue ethics?
choices: Confucianism and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
Hobbes's Leviathan and Rousseau's Social Contract
Bentham's and Mill's writings on utility
Kant's Groundwork and Locke's Second Treatise
questions.explain: Virtue ethics goes back to Confucius (5th century BC) and to Aristotle's idea of arete, or excellence (4th century BC). The other works are Enlightenment-era sources of the theories virtue ethics criticizes.

questions.q: What does virtue ethics claim the Enlightenment theories (Kantianism, utilitarianism, social contract theory) leave out?
choices: Moral education, moral wisdom, relationships, and emotions
Respect for the rights of individual persons
The need for universal and impartial moral rules
Careful attention to the consequences of actions
questions.explain: Virtue ethicists say these factors are central to living a moral life. Consequences, rights and universal rules are exactly what the Enlightenment theories do address.

questions.q: How are moral virtues, as opposed to intellectual virtues, developed?
choices: By memorizing a code of ethics
By habitually performing right actions
By calculating each choice's results
By studying logic and mathematics
questions.explain: Moral virtues, such as honesty, are deep-seated dispositions built by habit. Intellectual virtues are the ones associated with reasoning and truth.

questions.q: According to virtue ethics, what is a right action?
choices: What a virtuous person, acting in character, would do
Whatever respects everyone's negative rights
Whatever follows a rule that can be universalized
Whatever maximizes the total happiness of those affected
questions.explain: Virtue ethics defines right action through the virtuous person, someone who has and lives out the virtues needed to flourish.

questions.q: What is a vice, according to virtue ethics?
choices: A character trait that keeps a person from flourishing
An action with more harms than benefits
Any single action that breaks a law
A rule that cannot be universalized
questions.explain: Vices are the opposite of virtues: traits that prevent a person from flourishing or being truly happy. They are character traits, not individual acts or rules.

questions.q: Aristotle often places a virtue between two vices. Courage lies between cowardice and which vice?
choices: Prodigality
Rashness
Pride
Stinginess
questions.explain: Courage is the mean between cowardice and rashness. Prodigality and stinginess are the two extremes on either side of generosity.

questions.q: An employee wins a bonus and immediately gives all of it away to strangers, leaving herself unable to pay rent. Under virtue ethics, she has fallen into which vice?
choices: Cowardice
Stinginess
Prodigality
Rashness
questions.explain: Giving recklessly to excess is prodigality, one of the two vices on either side of generosity (the other is stinginess).

questions.q: Which argument supports virtue ethics, according to Quinn?
choices: It can easily be used to guide government policy
It allows precise numerical comparison of options
Everyone agrees on which traits count as virtues
It leaves no irresolvable moral dilemmas
questions.explain: Supporters also say personal relationships can be morally relevant, moral skill develops over time, and emotions matter. Guiding government policy is something Quinn says it cannot do.

questions.q: Which objection does Quinn raise against virtue ethics?
choices: It requires an impractical amount of calculation
It treats people merely as means to an end
It undermines holding people responsible for bad acts
It ignores the role of emotions in moral life
questions.explain: Quinn also notes that reasonable people may disagree about which traits are needed to flourish, and that virtue ethics cannot guide government policy. Ignoring emotions is a criticism virtue ethicists make of the Enlightenment theories.

questions.q: Leah posts an embarrassing photo of her friend Jamal on her popular blog without asking him. The analysis says real friendship requires reciprocity and equality, and that Leah took something from Jamal and put her own interests above his. Which theory is this?
choices: Social contract theory
Kantianism
Rule utilitarianism
Virtue ethics
questions.explain: Judging Leah by whether she acted like a good friend is a virtue ethics analysis. The social contract analysis of the same case focuses on Jamal's reasonable expectation of privacy.

questions.q: Eric Butler released Firesheep, a tool that made sidejacking easy, to pressure websites into fixing a security hole. One analysis praises his courage in taking responsibility for the tool and his benevolence in making it freely available. Which theory produced this analysis?
choices: Social contract theory
Kantianism
Virtue ethics
Act utilitarianism
questions.explain: Judging Butler by character traits like courage and benevolence is virtue ethics. The Kantian analysis condemns him for treating victims as means.

questions.q: How does Quinn distinguish ethical objectivism from relativism?
choices: Objectivism weighs consequences; relativism weighs duties and rights
Objectivism: morality exists outside the mind; relativism: it is a human invention
Objectivism governs individuals; relativism governs whole governments
Objectivism is religious in origin; relativism is entirely secular
questions.explain: This is Quinn's dividing line. Divine command theory, egoism, Kantianism, utilitarianism, social contract theory and virtue ethics are all objectivist.

questions.q: Which of these does Quinn treat as workable ethical theories?
choices: Divine command theory, act utilitarianism, and social contract theory
Ethical egoism, Kantianism, and virtue ethics only
Subjective relativism, cultural relativism, and divine command theory
Kantianism, utilitarianism (act and rule), social contract, virtue ethics
questions.explain: Quinn finds relativism, divine command theory and ethical egoism unworkable, and the remaining four (counting both forms of utilitarianism) workable.

questions.q: A theory says an action is right if it results in the maximum net increase in the total good of the affected parties. Which theory is it?
choices: Act utilitarianism
Virtue ethics
Social contract theory
Rule utilitarianism
questions.explain: Judging the act itself by its net good is act utilitarianism. Rule utilitarianism judges the rule the act falls under.

questions.q: A theory says an action is right if it follows a correct moral rule, and a rule is correct if everyone could follow it all the time without a logical contradiction that undermines the rule. Which theory is it?
choices: Social contract theory
Cultural relativism
Rule utilitarianism
Kantianism
questions.explain: Testing a rule for self-contradiction when universalized is Kant's first formulation. Rule utilitarianism tests rules by their total good.

questions.q: A theory says a moral rule is correct if rational people would collectively accept it as binding because of the benefits it brings the community. Which theory is it?
choices: Kantianism
Act utilitarianism
Social contract theory
Ethical egoism
questions.explain: Rules justified by rational, collective agreement for mutual benefit are the core of social contract theory.

questions.q: A theory says an action is right if it is consistent with the actions of a virtuous person. Which theory is it?
choices: Rule utilitarianism
Kantianism
Virtue ethics
Divine command theory
questions.explain: Virtue ethics looks to the virtuous person's character. It is the one workable theory that does not run through moral rules.

questions.q: Someone tests the rule 'I may break a law I believe to be unjust' and finds that if everyone acted on it, laws would be subverted, which contradicts their own wish to be treated justly. Which perspective is this?
choices: Act utilitarian
Virtue ethics
Kantian
Social contract
questions.explain: Universalizing the rule and finding a contradiction is Kant's method. The rule utilitarian version instead weighs harms such as lost respect for the law against the benefits.

questions.q: A rule utilitarian considers people ignoring laws they think are unjust. Which consequence does Quinn list as outweighing the benefits?
choices: A violation of the lawbreaker's own negative rights
A logical contradiction with wanting just treatment
A general loss of respect for the law
Damage to the lawbreaker's settled character traits
questions.explain: Rule utilitarianism weighs the consequences of the general practice: harm to people directly affected, loss of respect for law and a heavier burden on the justice system. The 'logical contradiction' answer is the Kantian argument.

questions.q: Which theory does Quinn show can, in some situations, approve of breaking the law?
choices: Kantianism
Rule utilitarianism
Act utilitarianism
Social contract theory
questions.explain: In the bedridden-friend CD example, act utilitarianism finds $25 of benefit and no harm. Kantianism, rule utilitarianism and social contract theory all support a strong obligation to obey.

questions.q: Which insight does Quinn attribute to Kantianism?
choices: A good person does right at the right time and way
It is wrong to privilege your own needs over others'
You should weigh consequences before deciding
We should collectively promote human rights
questions.explain: For Kantianism, every person is equally valuable and deserves respect as a rational being. Consequences belong to utilitarianism, human rights to social contract theory, and the good person to virtue ethics.

questions.q: What two questions does Quinn say you ultimately have to answer for yourself when making moral decisions?
choices: What does my culture believe, and what do most of my friends believe?
What kind of person do I want to be, and what kind of world do I want to live in?
What does the law require, and what will my employer be willing to accept?
What will maximize my income, and what will best protect my reputation?
questions.explain: Quinn ends Chapter 2 by encouraging readers to weigh duties, rights, consequences and virtues, and then to decide these two questions.

questions.q: How does Quinn define spam, and why is it so common?
choices: Coworker email on non-work topics; company servers make it free
Email carrying a virus; it spreads itself through address books
Unsolicited bulk email; about $10 reaches a million addresses
Email sent by government agencies; federal law requires it
questions.explain: Spam is unsolicited bulk email, and it is more than 30,000 times cheaper than paper junk mail. Viruses spread through email are malware, covered in Chapter 7.

questions.q: How much did spam grow during the 'spam tsunami'?
choices: From 50% of email in 2005 to 99% by 2015
From 9% of email in 2002 to 85% by 2009
From 1% of email in 1995 to 25% by 2000
From 30% of email in 2010 to 60% by 2020
questions.explain: The tsunami hit in 2003, and spam rose from 9% (2002) to 85% (2009) of email traffic.

questions.q: Anh, an accountant who distributes paychecks to all 50 employees, emails them all an ad for her daughter's Girl Scout cookie sale. One analysis says she didn't misrepresent anything or force anyone to read the email, so she didn't 'use' anyone and the act wasn't strictly wrong, though opt-in would have been better. Which theory is this?
choices: Kantianism
Rule utilitarianism
Act utilitarianism
Virtue ethics
questions.explain: Asking whether Anh treated her coworkers merely as means is the second formulation. The virtue analysis instead faults her for poor judgment and for not finding a role for her daughter.

questions.q: In the Anh cookie case, an analysis finds $108 in benefit to the Girl Scouts (36 boxes at $3 profit each) and $70 in lost productivity from complaining, and concludes the action was good. Which theory is this?
choices: Act utilitarianism
Kantianism
Social contract theory
Rule utilitarianism
questions.explain: Adding up dollar benefits and harms of this one act is act utilitarianism. The rule utilitarian analysis imagines everyone soliciting by email and concludes the act was wrong.

questions.q: An analysis of the Anh case asks what would happen if everyone in the company used email to solicit donations. It predicts grumbling, lower morale and few causes doing well, so it concludes Anh was wrong. Which theory is this?
choices: Kantianism (first formulation)
Cultural relativism
Rule utilitarianism
Act utilitarianism
questions.explain: Weighing the consequences of everyone following the practice is rule utilitarianism. A Kantian first-formulation test would look for a contradiction, not a balance of harms.

questions.q: In the Anh case, which theory concludes she did nothing wrong because Acme had no rule against such emails, she was exercising her right to express herself, and she didn't hide her identity or sell a fraudulent product?
choices: Divine command theory
Virtue ethics
Rule utilitarianism
Social contract theory
questions.explain: Reasoning about her rights and the absence of a prohibition is social contract theory. Quinn's summary suggests a sign-up sheet would have avoided the controversy.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the features of cryptocurrencies that Quinn lists?
choices: Unlimited transaction speed
Central bank backing
Guaranteed price stability
Decentralization
questions.explain: Quinn lists global accessibility, decentralization, anonymity, security and limited supply. Cryptocurrencies are independent of banks and highly volatile.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say Bitcoin will never replace credit card transactions?
choices: It requires every user to hold a bank account
It handles only about 3-7 transactions per second
It is illegal in nearly every country on earth
Its supply is unlimited, which causes inflation
questions.explain: Its throughput is far too low for global retail payments. Its supply is limited, not unlimited.

questions.q: What do 'proof of work' and 'proof of stake' refer to?
choices: Consensus protocols for adding blocks to a blockchain
Schemes for multifactor authentication
Exams used to certify software engineers
Methods for proving authorship of software
questions.explain: A blockchain lives on a distributed network, and every computer must agree on what to add. Proof of work and proof of stake are the two popular ways of reaching that agreement.

questions.q: Which text-messaging-based service in Kenya lets people save money, pay bills, transfer funds and check crop prices?
choices: Whisper
Parler
M-PESA
Kik Messenger
questions.explain: M-PESA shows how text messaging can transform lives where infrastructure is limited. Kik and Whisper are chat apps mentioned in connection with online predators.

questions.q: What is Quinn's basis for the concern that social media may harm democracy?
choices: Platforms refuse to carry any political content at all
Platforms are directly owned and run by governments
Very few Americans get any of their news from social media
Feeds match users' preferences, creating ideological echo chambers
questions.explain: Facebook supplies news to nearly half of Americans and builds preference profiles to keep users engaged, so people rarely see news that contradicts their worldview. That undermines a shared sense of reality.

questions.q: Why are police sting operations that pose as children online more likely to be accepted by a consequentialist than by others?
choices: Consequentialists consider deception a perfect duty
Consequentialists judge only the officers' character
Consequentialists give no weight to children's safety
Consequentialists weigh results like arrests over methods like deception
questions.explain: The goal is laudable, but the methods involve deception and revealing conversations people thought were private. Consequentialists weigh the outcomes most heavily.

questions.q: What did psychiatrist Jerald Block identify as the four characteristics of Internet addiction?
choices: Dopamine spikes, anxiety, insomnia, and depression
Stress, isolation, fear of failure, and peer pressure
Excessive use, withdrawal, tolerance, negative social consequences
Gaming, messaging, online shopping, and video streaming
questions.explain: Block also named three variants: excessive gaming, sexual preoccupations and messaging. Stress and fear of failure are among the contributing factors Quinn lists.

questions.q: How does Jeffrey Reiman's view of addiction differ from the Enlightenment view?
choices: Governments should respond by banning video games entirely
Society shares responsibility for putting people in hopeless situations
Addicts alone are fully responsible, since individuals govern their lives
Addiction is a purely genetic disease beyond anyone's control
questions.explain: Reiman says an addict's behavior makes sense if the addict has no hope for a better future. The Enlightenment view (Kantianism, utilitarianism, social contract theory) holds that individuals are responsible for their own choices.

questions.q: How does Quinn define censorship?
choices: The automatic removal of spam messages from users' email inboxes
A government's large-scale collection of data about its own citizens
An attempt to suppress or regulate public access to harmful or offensive material
Any law that restricts the sale of goods and services over the Internet
questions.explain: Censorship has traditionally been exercised by governments and religious institutions. The printing press broke their monopoly on distributing information.

questions.q: A government requires every radio and television station to get a license before it can broadcast. Which form of direct censorship is this?
choices: Prepublication review
Government monopolization
Self-censorship
Licensing and registration
questions.explain: Licensing is used to control media with limited bandwidth, such as radio and TV. Government monopolization means the state owns all the outlets, as in the former Soviet Union.

questions.q: According to Quinn, what is the most common form of censorship?
choices: Prepublication review
Self-censorship
Government monopolization
Web filtering
questions.explain: Groups often decide for themselves not to publish, to avoid persecution or to stay on good terms with official sources.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the challenges the Internet poses to censorship?
choices: It supports only one-to-many broadcasting
It is global and extends beyond national borders and laws
All of its content passes through one central server
It has too few websites to justify monitoring them
questions.explain: Quinn lists many-to-many communication, dynamic connections, a huge number of sites, global reach, and the difficulty of telling minors from adults. The Internet is decentralized, which is part of the challenge.

questions.q: Which country does Quinn describe as routing all Internet traffic through two government-controlled gateways that can block sites?
choices: Saudi Arabia
Germany
North Korea
United States
questions.explain: Saudi Arabia uses two gateways. In North Korea the Internet is virtually inaccessible, and Germany forbids access to neo-Nazi sites.

questions.q: Which of these is part of John Stuart Mill's argument against censorship?
choices: Censorship lowers the profits of printers and publishers
Have the courage to use your own reason without guidance
Censorship violates the commands revealed in scripture
No one is infallible, so truth emerges from a clash of ideas
questions.explain: Mill also argued that any opinion may contain a kernel of truth. 'Have the courage to use your own reason' is Kant's Enlightenment motto.

questions.q: What was the Court of Star Chamber?
choices: The congressional committee that drafted the First Amendment
An English court that enforced the anti-sedition law De Scandalis Magnatum
A medieval English guild that licensed every printing press
The Supreme Court panel that upheld the Child Internet Protection Act
questions.explain: The Star Chamber reported directly to the king and ignored traditional rules of evidence. People could be convicted for verbal insults or private writings.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say freedom of expression is not an absolute right?
choices: It is a positive right, and Quinn denies positive rights exist
It belongs only to the press and not to private individuals
The First Amendment protects only political speech, not other speech
It must be balanced against the public good, as in banning TV cigarette ads
questions.explain: Restrictions are justified when they produce a greater public good. The First Amendment covers both political and nonpolitical speech.

questions.q: Leah secretly photographs her friend Jamal wearing a rival party's T-shirt at a private party and posts it on her popular blog. One analysis says she treated Jamal as a means to her end of increasing her blog's readership. Which theory is this?
choices: Kantianism
Act utilitarianism
Social contract theory
Rule utilitarianism
questions.explain: Using Jamal merely as a means is the Kantian second formulation. The social contract analysis focuses on his reasonable expectation of privacy.

questions.q: In the Leah's blog case, the photo was taken at a private party in a friend's apartment. One analysis concludes Leah violated Jamal's right to privacy because he had a reasonable expectation of privacy there. Which theory is this?
choices: Kantianism
Act utilitarianism
Social contract theory
Virtue ethics
questions.explain: Reasoning about rights and reasonable expectations is social contract theory.

questions.q: In the Leah's blog case, which analysis concludes Leah did a good thing because both she and Jamal became more popular, while Jamal's anger was temporary and future harm was unlikely?
choices: Act utilitarianism
Kantianism
Rule utilitarianism
Social contract theory
questions.explain: Weighing the actual benefits and harms of this act is act utilitarianism. It is the only one of the five analyses that approves; the other four conclude Leah was wrong.

questions.q: What does the Child Internet Protection Act (CIPA) require, and how did the Supreme Court rule on it?
choices: All ISPs must block adult content; struck down 9-0 in 1997
Schools must monitor student email; never reviewed by the Court
Sites need parental consent for children; upheld 5-4 in 2010
Federally funded libraries must filter obscenity; upheld 6-3 in 2003
questions.explain: CIPA ties filtering of obscenity and child pornography to federal networking funds for libraries. In June 2003 the Supreme Court found it did not violate the First Amendment. Parental consent for children's data is COPPA, from Chapter 6.

questions.q: How do the ethical evaluations of CIPA differ?
choices: Every theory, including Kantianism, agrees that CIPA is morally right
Kantianism: wrong; act utilitarianism: depends; social contract: favors conscience
Act utilitarianism: clearly wrong; Kantianism: clearly right
Only virtue ethics concludes CIPA is wrong; the others all approve
questions.explain: Kantianism and social contract theory, which gives freedom of conscience precedence, both lean against CIPA, while the act utilitarian verdict depends on how benefits and harms are weighed.

questions.q: According to Locke's Second Treatise of Government, when do people have a right to things they remove from nature through their labor?
choices: Only when they share the property equally with all
Only when the government has granted them a patent
Whenever they pay fair market value for the materials
When no one claims more than they can use and plenty is left
questions.explain: Locke ties property rights to labor, with these two conditions. Quinn then asks whether this argument extends to intellectual property.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say the analogy between writing a play and making a belt buckle is imperfect?
choices: Plays are always written collaboratively, while buckles are made alone
Belt buckles cannot legally be sold, while plays can be sold freely
Two people can write the same play at once, and copying it leaves both with a copy
Writing a play takes far less labor than mining and casting a belt buckle
questions.explain: Unlike physical property, intellectual property can be created independently twice and copied without taking anything away. These two paradoxes weaken the case for a natural right to intellectual property.

questions.q: A soft-drink company keeps its formula confidential. It never expires, but competitors may legally try to reverse engineer it. What kind of protection is this?
choices: Patent
Copyright
Trade secret
Trademark
questions.explain: Trade secrets never expire and allow reverse engineering, but they can be compromised when employees leave. A patent would require public disclosure and expire after 20 years.

questions.q: A company's brand name becomes so widely used as a generic word for the product that the company risks losing legal protection for it. Which kind of intellectual property is at risk?
choices: Patent
Trademark
Trade secret
Copyright
questions.explain: A trademark can be lost if the brand name becomes a common noun, which is why companies advertise and contact people who misuse their marks.

questions.q: What does a patent give its owner?
choices: Five rights over an original expression lasting the author's life plus 70 years
Exclusive rights for 20 years, in exchange for publicly describing the invention
Rights to a brand name that last for as long as the name remains in use
Protection of a confidential process that never expires as long as it stays secret
questions.explain: A patent is a public document, and the owner can stop others from making, using or selling the invention for 20 years. A confidential, never-expiring protection describes a trade secret.

questions.q: What happened when Alexander Graham Bell's telephone patents expired in 1894?
choices: Telephones could no longer legally be leased
