The federal government nationalized phone service
AT&T was immediately split into the Baby Bells
About 6,000 local phone companies sprang up
questions.explain: Bell's patents had given the Bell Telephone Company a monopoly. The Baby Bells came much later, in 1984, after a 1974 antitrust suit.

questions.q: A studio turns a copyrighted novel into a film without permission. Which of the copyright owner's five rights has been infringed?
choices: Public performance of the work
Production of derivative works
Distribution of copies
Public display of the work
questions.explain: Copyright gives five rights: reproduction, distribution, public display, public performance and the production of derivative works. A film adaptation is a derivative work.

questions.q: What does the No Electronic Theft Act do?
choices: Outlaws circumventing encryption placed on digital media
Criminalizes copying over $1,000 of copyrighted material in six months
Requires public libraries to filter pornographic web pages
Lets consumers make backup copies of music recordings
questions.explain: The NET Act criminalized large-scale infringement even without profit. Circumventing encryption is the DMCA, and backup copies are covered by the Audio Home Recording Act.

questions.q: In Gershwin Publishing v. Columbia Artists, why was Columbia Artists Management held liable?
choices: For infringements by concert associations it supported
For manufacturing and selling portable MP3 players
For posting software on a computer bulletin board
For operating a peer-to-peer music network
questions.explain: Columbia Artists was held liable for infringement by community concert groups it helped organize. Posting software on a bulletin board was the Davey Jones Locker case against Richard Kenadek.

questions.q: Rajiv signed a confidentiality agreement at Felicity Software and has moved to Unrelated.com. If he gets 'personally involved' and asks his new team leading questions that reveal his old optimizations, why does the Kantian analysis say he acts wrongly?
choices: Good managers never share their expertise with teams
It would delay the product release by six months
Breaking his signed agreement is breaking a promise
His new company would earn less money as a result
questions.explain: Kantianism treats the confidentiality agreement as a promise. The 'clean room' option, which uses only public information and performance targets, follows a rule that can be universalized: share your expertise with others.

questions.q: Which conclusion does Quinn reach about Rajiv's two options?
choices: Only act utilitarianism favors involvement; the other theories favor the clean room
Every one of the theories, including act utilitarianism, favors the clean room
Only virtue ethics favors the clean room; the rest favor getting involved
Every one of the theories favors getting personally involved with the team
questions.explain: The act utilitarian dollar calculation narrowly favors getting personally involved, though a more risk-averse calculation would favor the clean room. Kantianism, social contract theory and virtue ethics all favor the clean room.

questions.q: When courts judge whether a use of a copyrighted work is fair use, which four factors do they consider?
choices: Purpose of use, nature of work, amount copied, effect on market
Author's intent, number of copies, format, and country of use
Registration status, price, length, and popularity of the work
Author's nationality, work's age, copier's income, and medium
questions.explain: These four factors decide fair use. Under current law a work is copyrighted the moment it is created, so registration is not a factor.

questions.q: You record a TV broadcast to watch later at home, and separately make a copy of a CD you own to give to a friend. How does copyright law treat these two acts?
choices: Time shifting is fair use; copying for a friend is not
Neither act qualifies as fair use
Both acts qualify as fair use
Copying for a friend is fair use; time shifting is not
questions.explain: The Supreme Court held that recording broadcasts for later private viewing (time shifting) is fair use. Making a copy for a friend is not, even though space shifting your own music to a portable player is.

questions.q: In RIAA v. Diamond Multimedia, what did the Ninth Circuit decide about Diamond's Rio MP3 player?
choices: MP3 compression is itself a form of copyright infringement
Owners must pay a royalty for each song moved to the player
The Rio violated the Audio Home Recording Act and was banned
Space shifting music to a portable device is legal
questions.explain: The RIAA sued under the Audio Home Recording Act, but the court affirmed that space shifting is consistent with copyright law. The AHRA itself requires digital recorders to include SCMS to block copies of copies.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act's (DMCA) provisions?
choices: The length of copyright protection was shortened
Consumers may make backup copies of any digital media
Circumventing copy controls is illegal, even for fair use
Noncommercial peer-to-peer file sharing was legalized
questions.explain: The DMCA, the first big revision of copyright law since 1976, extended copyright length and outlawed circumventing encryption and copy controls. The right to make backup copies comes from the Audio Home Recording Act.

questions.q: Why did the Secure Digital Music Initiative (SDMI) fail?
choices: Its digital watermarking was cracked, and Internet copying got there first
The major record labels refused to join the industry consortium
Congress outlawed the use of digital watermarking in consumer products
The technology worked well but was far too expensive for consumers
questions.explain: The consortium of about 200 companies could not get ahead of Internet copying, some sponsors were electronics companies, and the watermark scheme was broken.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the criticisms of digital rights management (DRM) that Quinn lists?
choices: It applies only to analog media
It undermines fair use
It is unbreakable, so owners are too powerful
It makes content too easy to copy
questions.explain: Critics also say DRM could reduce competition, some schemes make anonymous access impossible, and any technological 'fix' is bound to fail. DRM restricts copying, so 'too easy to copy' gets it backwards.

questions.q: What happened to Napster?
choices: It won its lawsuit against the RIAA and stayed a free file-sharing network
BitTorrent acquired it, and it was turned into a cyberlocker service
The RIAA won in court; it went offline in 2001 and returned as a paid service
The FBI shut it down in 1995 for distributing pirated business software
questions.explain: Napster began as a peer-to-peer music exchange in 1999, went offline in July 2001 and re-emerged in 2003 as a subscription service. Its centralized index made it easy for courts to shut down.

questions.q: Why was FastTrack, the technology behind KaZaA and Grokster, harder to shut down than Napster?
choices: It charged every user a monthly subscription
Every file it shared was encrypted with DRM
It operated only from outside the United States
Its index was spread across many 'super nodes'
questions.explain: Second-generation peer-to-peer networks decentralized the index, so there was no single point to shut down.

questions.q: How does BitTorrent speed up downloads of large files?
choices: It downloads different pieces of a file from many peers at once
It buys priority routing through tiered Internet service
It stores each file on one high-speed central server
It compresses every file to 10% of its original size
questions.explain: Broadband downloads faster than it uploads, so pulling pieces from many peers at once fills the download pipe. Compressing audio to about 10% of its size is what MP3 does.

questions.q: What does a software copyright protect?
choices: The source code, but never the object program
The expression of an idea, such as the object program
Any software process with practical utility
The underlying algorithm or idea itself
questions.explain: Copyright covers expression, not ideas, and companies often keep source code as a trade secret. A process with practical utility is what a software patent covers.

questions.q: How do software copyrights differ from software patents?
choices: Copyright is costly and slow to obtain; a patent is cheap and quick to obtain
Patents protect screen displays, while copyrights protect useful processes
Copyright is cheap and allows reverse engineering; a patent is costly and doesn't
Both copyrights and patents fully allow reverse engineering of software
questions.explain: Quinn's comparison table shows copyright is quick and inexpensive and protects the object program and screen displays. Patents are expensive and time-consuming and protect processes with practical utility.

questions.q: When did the U.S. Patent Office start granting software patents, and why had it refused before?
choices: In 1981; it had viewed programs as mathematical algorithms
Never; software has always been excluded from patents
In 1998, as one of the provisions of the DMCA
In 1964, at the same time software copyrights began
questions.explain: A Supreme Court decision led to the first software patent in 1981, and later rulings widened the scope. Before then the office saw programs as algorithms, not processes or machines. Software copyright began in 1964.

questions.q: To avoid unconsciously copying a competitor, Team 1 analyzes the competitor's program and writes a specification, and a separate Team 2 builds new software only from that specification. What is this strategy called?
choices: Reverse engineering for distribution
Copyleft licensing
Space shifting
Clean room software development
questions.explain: Reverse engineering is allowed, and the clean room approach protects the company against charges of copying. Copyleft is an open-source licensing idea.

questions.q: Which of these is part of the open-source definition?
choices: Only the original developer may modify the source
Users must pay a subscription to receive updates
The same rights pass to everyone receiving redistributions
The software may be used only for noncommercial ends
questions.explain: This 'copyleft' rule sits alongside including the source code and allowing anyone to modify, sell or give away the software. 'Noncommercial only' would itself be a restriction on use.

questions.q: Who started the GNU Project, and who wrote the Linux kernel?
choices: Tim Berners-Lee started GNU (1989); Vint Cerf wrote Linux (1993)
Linus Torvalds started GNU (1984); Richard Stallman wrote Linux (1991)
Richard Stallman started GNU (1984); Linus Torvalds wrote Linux (1991)
Steve Wozniak started GNU (1976); Bill Gates wrote Linux (1985)
questions.explain: GNU aimed to build an open-source, Unix-like operating system. Torvalds's kernel combined with GNU components gave the system commonly called Linux.

questions.q: A smartphone maker controls exactly which apps users may install, which lets it enforce security standards and earn revenue from app sales. Which type of platform is this, and what is Quinn's example?
choices: An open-source platform, like Linux
A closed platform, like Apple's iOS
An open platform, like Google's Android
A cyberlocker service, like Dropbox
questions.explain: Closed platforms (walled gardens) provide a consistent experience and security control. Open platforms, such as Android, encourage more developers, lower prices and no lock-in.

questions.q: What problem does a Creative Commons license solve?
choices: It blocks all copying of the work, including fair-use copying
It says in advance which kinds of copying are allowed, speeding reuse
It places a work permanently and irrevocably in the public domain
It registers the work with the Copyright Office for legal protection
questions.explain: Works are copyrighted the moment they are created, so without a license people must contact the creator before reusing them. A CC license spells out which rights are kept. Flickr hosts more than 250 million CC-licensed photos.

questions.q: Who said 'You have zero privacy anyway. Get over it.'?
choices: Edward Snowden
Judith Jarvis Thomson
Scott McNealy
Louis Brandeis
questions.explain: Quinn opens Chapter 5 with Sun Microsystems CEO Scott McNealy's remark and asks whether privacy is important and whether it can be protected.

questions.q: How does Quinn's discussion define privacy?
choices: As a perfect duty that each person owes to themselves
As the legal right to own and sell personal property
As a 'zone of inaccessibility' limiting access to a person
As the right to hide one's income from the government
questions.explain: Access can be physical proximity to a person or knowledge about them. Privacy violations are an affront to human dignity, but too much privacy can also harm society.

questions.q: Which of these does Quinn list as a harm of privacy?
choices: It can hide dysfunctional families
It makes people less self-reliant
It prevents intimate relationships
It blocks growth as a unique person
questions.explain: Privacy can also cover illegal or immoral acts, burden the nuclear family and let people on society's fringes be ignored. The other three options reverse benefits of privacy that Quinn lists.

questions.q: What did Warren and Brandeis argue in their 1890 article 'The Right to Privacy'?
choices: People have zero privacy and should accept it
Every privacy violation also violates another right
Privacy is a prudential right, not a natural one
Law should protect the 'right to be let alone'
questions.explain: Warren was upset by newspaper coverage of his daughter's wedding. Their phrase 'the right to be let alone' became influential in American courts. The 'another right' option is Thomson's argument.

questions.q: What is Judith Jarvis Thomson's argument against a natural right to privacy?
choices: Privacy rights were created by the Third Amendment
Privacy grew out of property rights, so it is natural
Privacy is needed for personal growth, so it is natural
Every privacy violation also violates some other right
questions.explain: Thomson also says defining privacy as 'the right to be let alone' is too narrow (it misses covert spying) and too broad (it includes assault), so there is no need to define privacy rights precisely. The property-rights origin is an argument in favor of a natural right.

questions.q: What is Quinn's own position on whether there is a right to privacy?
choices: It exists only where the Constitution names it explicitly
No right to privacy of any kind exists for anyone
It is a prudential right recognized because it benefits society
It is an absolute natural right that can never be limited
questions.explain: Privacy is not a natural right, but rational people agree to recognize some privacy rights because doing so benefits society, which fits the social contract approach. The Do Not Call Registry is a later example.

questions.q: Meena and Alex secretly monitor their nanny through a laptop camera. One analysis tests the rule 'An employer may secretly monitor an employee who works with vulnerable people' and finds that, universalized, no employee would expect privacy, so secret monitoring would be impossible. Which theory is this?
choices: Social contract theory
Virtue ethics
Kantianism
Rule utilitarianism
questions.explain: A rule that defeats itself when universalized fails Kant's first formulation. The rule utilitarian analysis instead predicts stressed nannies and higher turnover.

questions.q: In the new parents case, which theory concludes that secretly monitoring the nanny can be seen as characteristic of good parents protecting a defenseless baby, while expecting them to stop once they are sure the nanny is doing well?
choices: Virtue ethics
Rule utilitarianism
Kantianism
Social contract theory
questions.explain: Virtue ethics is the only one of the four analyses that finds the monitoring defensible. Kantianism, rule utilitarianism and social contract theory all conclude it was wrong.

questions.q: A deed to a house, a marriage license and a criminal conviction are all reported to government agencies so the public can be informed. What are they?
choices: Trade secrets
Secondary uses of information
Public records
Privately held information
questions.explain: Public records inform the public, and computerized databases and the Internet have made them much easier to reach.

questions.q: A search engine uses your past search history to decide that your query 'bass' means fishing rather than music. Information collected for one purpose (logging searches) is being used for another (personalizing results). What is this called?
choices: Opt-in consent
Secondary use
Collaborative filtering
Sidejacking
questions.explain: Secondary use means using information for a purpose other than the one it was collected for. Collaborative filtering predicts one person's preferences from the preferences of many others.

questions.q: Why do direct marketing organizations prefer opt-out policies over opt-in policies?
choices: Opt-in requires prior permission, a barrier for new businesses
Opt-out guarantees that consumers are never contacted
Opt-in actually lets marketers share more information
Opt-out is the approach mandated by the GDPR in Europe
questions.explain: Under opt-out, organizations can share information until a consumer forbids it, while opt-in puts the burden on them to get permission first. The GDPR leans toward requiring permission, the opposite of opt-out.

questions.q: What does the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) require companies to do?
choices: Delete all customer data after 30 days of storage
Disclose what they collect and why, and get permission first
Store all personal data on servers inside the U.S.
Sell customer data only to companies based in the EU
questions.explain: In response, many American companies added website banners asking users for consent.

questions.q: How did Target use data mining in its pregnancy-prediction effort?
choices: It sold a CD of household data to small businesses for mailings
It predicted second-trimester customers from purchases like unscented lotion
It required pregnant customers to register for loyalty discounts
It tracked shoppers' cell phones as they moved through its stores
questions.explain: Target then mixed baby-product offers in with unrelated items. New parents' shopping habits are unusually easy to change, which makes them valuable targets. Tracking shoppers' phones is the 2011 mall case.

questions.q: Why did Lotus Development Corporation drop its plan to sell its Marketplace: Households CD?
choices: Congress passed a law banning mailing lists
The FTC fined Lotus for violating COPPA
The CD's data was found to be inaccurate
Over 30,000 consumers complained about privacy
questions.explain: The CD held information on 120 million Americans. It is Quinn's classic example of consumer backlash.

questions.q: Telemarketers repeatedly call a family during dinner. Under Solove's taxonomy of privacy, which category does this fall into?
choices: Invasion
Information collection
Information dissemination
Information processing
questions.explain: Invasion covers activities that intrude on daily life or disturb someone's solitude. Dissemination is the spreading of personal information.

questions.q: What does the Employee Polygraph Protection Act of 1988 do?
choices: Bars most private employers from using lie detector tests
Lets any employer require a polygraph for hiring
Requires every federal employee to take lie detector tests
Bans lie detector results from all criminal trials
questions.explain: There are exceptions: pharmaceutical and security firms may test certain employees, and employers who have suffered a theft can test reasonable suspects. Federal, state and local governments are exempt.

questions.q: Under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), what must online services do?
choices: Delete all data collected about any user younger than 18
Filter content inappropriate for minors in all public libraries
Get parental consent before collecting data from children 12 and under
Verify every user's age with a government-issued identification
questions.explain: Epic Games paid a $275 million settlement in 2022 over collecting information from children playing Fortnite. Library filtering is CIPA.

questions.q: Which of these is a limit of the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA)?
choices: It lets large employers use genetic data when hiring
It does not cover life insurance, and small firms are exempt
It protects only employees of the federal government
It lets health insurers request genetic test results
questions.explain: GINA bars health insurers and most employers from using genetic information, but it does not apply to life, disability or long-term care insurance, and employers with fewer than 15 employees are exempt.

questions.q: When did the Census Bureau break its confidentiality requirement during wartime, according to Quinn?
choices: In the Civil War, to locate people who had escaped slavery
In the Vietnam War, to track antiwar protesters
After 9/11, to identify immigrants from Muslim countries
In both World Wars, including the internment of Japanese Americans
questions.explain: In World War I census information helped find draft resisters, and in World War II the Army used it to round up Japanese Americans. These are Quinn's examples of how data collected for one purpose can be misused.

questions.q: The FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) helped tie James Earl Ray to the assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and helped catch which bomber?
choices: Richard Reid (shoe bomber)
Ted Kaczynski (Unabomber)
Timothy McVeigh (Oklahoma City)
The Boston Marathon bombers
questions.explain: NCIC is a collection of 21 databases. Surveillance camera images, not NCIC, were key in the Boston Marathon case.

questions.q: What is the criticism of the National Data Exchange (N-DEx)?
choices: It contains information only about convicted felons
It shares information on people never charged with a crime
The Supreme Court has ruled it unconstitutional
Its data can be accessed by the FBI and no one else
questions.explain: N-DEx shares incident reports, arrest reports and interrogation summaries that are not available through NCIC, and there is no way to correct misinformation in raw police reports.

questions.q: What problem with police use of facial recognition does Quinn highlight?
choices: Facial recognition has never produced a single false match
Federal law lets police treat any match as probable cause
Congress has banned all police use of facial recognition nationwide
Some officers arrest on a match alone, and errors are higher for darker skin
questions.explain: A match is supposed to be only a lead, not probable cause. Several innocent Black men have been jailed, and about two dozen states and cities banned police use, though some bans were later dropped.

questions.q: Which 1986 law allows police to attach a pen register or a trap-and-trace device to a suspect's phone line with a court order, without showing probable cause?
choices: Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control Act
The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act
The Electronic Communications Privacy Act
The Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act
questions.explain: The ECPA also allows roving wiretaps. A pen register shows the number being dialed, and a trap-and-trace device shows the caller's number.

questions.q: Investigators want emails a suspect has stored with an ISP. Under the Stored Communications Act, what is true of messages more than 180 days old?
choices: The ISP is required to destroy them
Only a FISA Court order can release them
They require a warrant based on probable cause
The government can get them without a warrant
questions.explain: This part of the ECPA was written before cloud email. The Digital Due Process coalition has lobbied to change it.

questions.q: What did Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 allow?
choices: The NSA may intercept international calls without any warrant
Police with a court order may tap a phone for up to 30 days
The FBI may issue National Security Letters without a judge
Foreign nationals may be watched for a year without a court order
questions.explain: In 1972 the Supreme Court again rejected warrantless wiretapping, even for national security. One year without a court order is a FISA provision.

questions.q: What did documents leaked by Edward Snowden reveal about the PRISM program?
choices: The TSA saved detailed body-scanner images of travelers
The NSA had access to servers at firms like Google and Apple
The FBI used Carnivore to read millions of domestic emails
The NSA kept phone records first revealed by USA Today
questions.explain: PRISM let the NSA monitor communications of foreigners outside the U.S. through companies such as Microsoft, Google, Facebook and Apple, which all denied knowing about it. The phone records database is a separate NSA program, from 2006.

questions.q: What are National Security Letters, created under the USA PATRIOT Act?
choices: Requests from foreign governments for U.S. intelligence
Notices warning citizens that they are under surveillance
FBI demands for records, issued without a judge or probable cause
Court orders that authorize a wiretap for up to 30 days
questions.explain: The FBI can collect library, medical, business and other records this way, and gag orders keep recipients, such as libraries, from saying they received one. The FBI issued about 50,000 a year from 2003 to 2006.

questions.q: After the 2004 Madrid train bombings, the FBI wrongly linked a partial fingerprint to an Oregon lawyer, secretly searched his home, and detained him for two weeks before Spanish authorities matched the print to an Algerian. Whose case is this?
choices: Richard Reid
Terry Dean Rogan
John Walker Lindh
Brandon Mayfield
questions.explain: The government apologized and paid Mayfield $2 million. It is Quinn's example of a PATRIOT Act failure. Terry Dean Rogan was a victim of identity theft and false arrest, covered in Chapter 8.

questions.q: Which of these is a principle of the Code of Fair Information Practices?
choices: Only private companies are bound by it
Uses may change without the person's consent
There must be no secret databases
Agencies may freely share all records
questions.explain: The code also says people should have access to their records and be able to correct them, and that database owners are responsible for reliability and preventing misuse.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say the Privacy Act of 1974 falls short?
choices: It covers only government databases and lets agencies share records
It applies only to the files kept by private credit bureaus
It requires every database to be deleted after seven years
It was struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court
questions.explain: It also covers only records indexed by a personal ID and has no federal employee responsible for enforcing it, which makes it much weaker than the Code of Fair Information Practices.

questions.q: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, how long may negative information generally stay on a credit report?
choices: 3 years (bankruptcies 5; convictions 10 years)
10 years (bankruptcies 15; convictions 20 years)
7 years (bankruptcies 10; convictions indefinitely)
Indefinitely, with no exceptions for any item
questions.explain: The FCRA promotes the accuracy and privacy of information held by credit bureaus such as Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.

questions.q: What does the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act (2004) give consumers?
choices: A credit report mailed automatically to every consumer each month
The right to have any negative information deleted from reports
A ban on credit bureaus selling reports to banks and lenders
A free credit report from each major bureau every 12 months, on request
questions.explain: Consumers have to ask for their reports. The act also includes provisions to reduce identity theft.

questions.q: The Financial Services Modernization Act (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, 1999) created 'financial supermarkets'. Which privacy provision does it include?
choices: Banks are forbidden to sell insurance
Customers may sue over any data breach
Privacy notices must include an opt-out clause
Customers must opt in before any sharing
questions.explain: Privacy policies must be disclosed, and companies must protect confidential information. The act uses opt-out, which marketers prefer, rather than opt-in.

questions.q: The IRS compares the income on a tax return with what employers and banks report for the same person. Which technique is this?
choices: Collaborative filtering
Syndromic surveillance
Computer matching
Microtargeting
questions.explain: Computer matching checks forms against outside sources. The IRS also uses data mining to search returns for patterns that suggest errors leading to underpayment.

questions.q: What is a syndromic surveillance system?
choices: A database of people placed on the terrorist watch list
Data mining that looks for signs of an epidemic or bioterrorism
A system that tracks license plates on public highways
A program that monitors international telephone calls
questions.explain: Such systems scan 911 calls, ER visits, school absences and Internet searches. At the start of COVID-19 in 2020, an Arizona system spotted a rise in methanol poisonings, which led the FDA to recall some hand sanitizers.

questions.q: Why does Quinn call the Social Security number a poor identification number?
choices: It is too long for most people to remember reliably
It isn't unique, is rarely checked, and has no error detection
It encodes sensitive biometric data about the holder
It changes every time a person moves to a new state
questions.explain: SSNs were first issued in 1936 for Social Security only, and their use has gradually expanded.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the arguments against a national ID card that Quinn presents?
choices: No other democracies use such cards
No card positively guarantees identification
It would make illegal entry much easier
Current ID cards are already excellent
questions.explain: Opponents add that insiders can compromise even hard-to-forge cards, no biometric system is 100% accurate, and a national ID makes government data mining simpler. Supporters argue current IDs are second-rate and other democracies have national cards.

questions.q: What does the Real ID Act (signed May 2005) require of new driver's licenses?
choices: Nothing for flying, since licenses are no longer needed to board
An implanted RFID chip carried by every licensed driver
The holder's Social Security number printed on the front
Four forms of ID to apply, plus a biometric identifier on the license
questions.explain: Licenses must also carry machine-readable data, and compliant licenses are needed for domestic flights. Quinn says that once every state complies, the U.S. will effectively have a national ID card.

questions.q: A 20-year-old college student asks to review her educational records and have an error corrected, and she objects to their release without her permission. Which law protects these rights?
choices: FOIA
HIPAA
The Privacy Act of 1974
FERPA
questions.explain: The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act gives these rights to students 18 and older and to the parents of younger students. HIPAA covers medical information.

questions.q: Which statement about the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is accurate?
choices: It applies equally to all three branches of government
It was passed after 9/11 to expand surveillance powers
It restricts how hospitals may share patients' records
Signed by Johnson in 1966, it covers only the executive branch
questions.explain: FOIA has nine exemptions, such as classified documents. It is an example of information dissemination meant to give the public access to government records.

questions.q: Why does Quinn call the National Do Not Call Registry an example of privacy treated as a prudential right?
choices: Its benefit was judged to outweigh the harm of limiting ads
It was created by a court ruling, not by an agency
The Constitution explicitly bans unwanted phone calls
Telemarketing was legally found to be a form of fraud
questions.explain: Shielding people from telemarketers was judged worth more than unrestricted telephone advertising. The FTC created the registry in 2003, and more than 50 million numbers were registered before it took effect.

questions.q: What happened with the TSA's Advanced Imaging Technology (AIT) body scanners?
choices: After EPIC sued, scanners showing passenger-specific images were gone by 2013
They were replaced at airports by ID checks for pseudoephedrine
Congress banned every airport body scanner in the United States in 2007
Courts ordered all scanner images saved for criminal investigations
questions.explain: The first AIT scanners showed anatomical features in detail, and EPIC's 2010 suit claimed Fourth Amendment violations. The TSA moved to generic outlines.

questions.q: An attacker phones a company's help desk pretending to be a panicked executive who forgot his password and talks the technician into resetting it. Which hacking technique is this?
choices: Brute-force search
Dumpster diving
Social engineering
Dictionary attack
questions.explain: Manipulating people into revealing credentials is social engineering. A dictionary attack automatically tries common words as passwords.

questions.q: Why is multifactor authentication effective, according to Quinn?
choices: A stolen password alone is not enough to log in
It makes passwords completely unnecessary
It stops users from ever reusing a password
It encrypts all of a user's network traffic
questions.explain: MFA requires two or more authenticators, such as a password plus a code texted to your phone, and Microsoft says it blocks more than 99.9% of account-compromise attacks, unless you are tricked into revealing the code.

questions.q: What is the maximum penalty under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act?
choices: Civil fines only, with no prison time
20 years in prison and a $250,000 fine
5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine
Life in prison without parole
questions.explain: The CFAA criminalizes accessing Internet-connected computers without authorization, transmitting damaging code, trafficking in passwords, computer fraud and extortion.

questions.q: What is sidejacking?
choices: Hijacking a Web session by capturing a user's cookie
Injecting a client-side script into a shared website
Inserting a SQL query into a form to steal data
Getting malware just by visiting a compromised site
questions.explain: Sidejacking is possible on unencrypted wireless networks because many sites sent cookies 'in the clear'. Injecting a client-side script into a site is cross-site scripting.

questions.q: Eric Butler's Firesheep (October 2010) led Facebook and Twitter to offer secure connections within months, with no evidence of a big rise in identity theft. Which theory concludes, on these grounds, that releasing it was good?
choices: Act utilitarianism
Rule utilitarianism
Social contract theory
Kantianism
questions.explain: High benefits and minimal harms make it good on the act utilitarian view. The Kantian analysis condemns Butler for treating victims as a means to his end.

questions.q: Which analysis says Firesheep's release was wrong because Butler accepted a short-term rise in privacy violations to pressure websites, treating the victims as a means to his end?
choices: Kantianism
Virtue ethics
Cultural relativism
Act utilitarianism
questions.explain: Using victims as mere means is the second formulation. Kantians also hold Butler partly accountable for wrongs that others committed with his tool.

questions.q: A program attaches itself to other executable files on the same computer and runs whenever its host program runs. A different program is self-contained and spreads across a network by exploiting security holes. What are these two programs?
choices: Two Trojan horses
A virus, then a worm
A rootkit, then a bot
A worm, then a virus
questions.explain: A virus is self-replicating code embedded in a host program. A worm is self-contained and spreads through networks.

questions.q: Which statement about Robert Tappan Morris Jr.'s Internet worm is accurate?
choices: A Cornell student, he released it from MIT and got probation and fines
A defense contractor, he released it and was sentenced to 20 years in prison
A hacker, he released it in 2003 specifically to remove the Blaster worm
A Stanford professor, he released it to test antivirus tools and was never charged
questions.explain: The worm crashed many Unix computers. Morris got 3 years' probation, 400 hours of community service and $150,000 in legal fees and fines. Releasing it from MIT instead of Cornell is why the virtue ethics analysis calls him deceitful. Removing Blaster in 2003 was the Nachi worm.

questions.q: A free screensaver works as advertised but secretly gives an attacker remote access to the victim's computer. What is it?
choices: A rootkit
Adware
A backdoor Trojan
A network worm
questions.explain: A Trojan horse hides a sinister purpose behind a harmless function, and a backdoor Trojan gives the attacker access. A rootkit's defining trait is using privileged access to hide itself.

questions.q: Malware encrypts every file on a hospital's computers and demands payment for the decryption key. What kind of malware is it?
choices: Ransomware
A rootkit
Spyware
A drive-by download
questions.explain: Modern ransomware encrypts files and demands payment. A drive-by download is one way it can get installed, not the malware itself.

questions.q: What is a botnet?
choices: A peer-to-peer music-sharing network run by the RIAA
A network of volunteer computers run by a system administrator
A cluster of antivirus servers operated by Microsoft
Bot-infected computers run by one command-and-control program
questions.explain: The person who controls a botnet is a bot herder. Some botnets have more than a million computers and are used to send spam and launch distributed denial-of-service attacks.

questions.q: An attacker sends carefully crafted emails only to the accounting staff of one company, pretending to be the CFO and asking for login credentials. What is this?
choices: Phishing
Spear-phishing
SQL injection
A denial-of-service attack
questions.explain: Spear-phishing selects its recipients to target a particular group. Ordinary phishing is a large-scale, untargeted effort.

questions.q: Which statement about the 2021 Colonial Pipeline attack is accurate?
choices: The company refused to pay, and the pipeline never shut down
North Korea launched it as a DDoS attack over the Fourth of July
Hackers got in with a reused password and were paid a Bitcoin ransom
Hackers used the Stuxnet worm to wreck the pipeline's centrifuges
questions.explain: The password had been exposed in another attack. The hackers encrypted data and demanded about $4 million in Bitcoin, the company paid, and the FBI later recovered $3.7 million. The decryption tool was too slow, so Colonial restored from backups.

questions.q: What did the Stuxnet worm (2009) attack?
choices: Twitter and Facebook on the anniversary of the Georgia war
Siemens SCADA systems at Iranian uranium enrichment sites
Unix computers on the early Internet in 1988
Estonian government and bank websites in 2007
questions.explain: Stuxnet, developed by the United States and Israel, temporarily shut down Iran's nuclear program. It shows the risk of SCADA systems being built on open Internet Protocol.

questions.q: What are the two kinds of data-related failure in computerized systems?
choices: Wrong data is entered, or retrieved data is misread
Hackers steal data, or insiders leak it
Hardware overheats, or the software crashes
Networks slow down, or servers lose power
questions.explain: Quinn's false-arrest cases show both kinds. Failures can also happen when the data is correct, if the program has an error.

questions.q: Someone stole a man's identity, and as a result he was arrested five times, three of them at gunpoint. He later received an award of about $55,000. Who is he?
choices: Terry Dean Rogan
Brandon Mayfield
Joshua Brown
Roberto Hernandez
questions.explain: Rogan's $55,000 award is the harm figure used in the act utilitarian analysis of the NCIC stolen-vehicle database. Roberto Hernandez was arrested twice because he was confused with another man of the same name.

questions.q: An analysis estimates the NCIC stolen-vehicle database recovers 100,000 cars a year at $5,000 of benefit each ($500 million), against about one false arrest a year costing $55,000, and concludes the database is good. Which theory is this?
choices: Rule utilitarianism
Social contract theory
Kantianism
Act utilitarianism
questions.explain: Weighing dollar benefits against harms for this particular system is act utilitarianism. Benefits exceed harms by about $499,945,000 a year.

questions.q: Amazon's British site mistakenly listed a handheld computer at a 97.5% markdown, then refused to deliver unless buyers paid the true price. One analysis imagines the rule 'A company must always honor the advertised price' and predicts higher costs and prices for all consumers. What does this analysis conclude, and which theory is it?
choices: Kantianism; Amazon wrongly broke a promise
Act utilitarianism; Amazon should have honored it
Social contract theory; buyers had a right to it
Rule utilitarianism; Amazon did the right thing
questions.explain: The rule has more harms than benefits. The Kantian analysis also sides with Amazon, arguing that the buyers knew it was an error and were not acting in good faith.

questions.q: Why did a Patriot missile battery fail to intercept a Scud missile that killed 28 soldiers in the 1991 Gulf War?
choices: A single wrong line of code sat in an error-recovery routine
An operator overrode a warning and entered the wrong coordinates
A race condition occurred between two concurrent software tasks
Over 100 hours of use let tiny truncation errors grow into a clock error
questions.explain: The system was designed to run only a few hours at a time. The clock drifted by 0.3433 seconds, which threw tracking off by hundreds of meters. A wrong line in an error-recovery routine caused the AT&T network failure.

questions.q: What caused the AT&T long-distance network failure, in which about half the switches crashed and 70 million calls failed?
choices: One bad line of error-recovery code, shared by most switches
A citywide power outage that started in New York City
A distributed denial-of-service attack by outside hackers
Operators who overrode repeated computer warnings
questions.explain: A switch rebooted and sent 'OK' messages, which made busy switches crash and reboot in turn. Because most switches ran the same software, the failure cascaded.

questions.q: Which factor does Quinn give for the failure of the Denver International Airport automated baggage system?
choices: The airport was designed before the baggage system was chosen
Reliance on a single sensor to route every piece of luggage
A race condition in the software controlling the bag scanners
Hackers who took remote control of the conveyor belts
questions.explain: The timeline was also too short and the system too complex for the development team. The airport opened 16 months late at a cost of $1 million a day, and a conventional baggage system had to be added.

questions.q: Which design decision made the Therac-25 more dangerous than its predecessors, the Therac-6 and Therac-20?
choices: Patients and technicians had to share the same room
It was the first such machine with any computer control
It used vacuum tubes in place of transistors
Hardware safety features were replaced with software
questions.explain: It also reused code from the earlier models. Without hardware interlocks, software errors such as race conditions could cause massive overdoses. Quinn draws the lesson that code reuse does not always mean higher quality.

questions.q: In the Therac-25, a fast operator could edit the prescription from X-ray to electron beam while the magnets were still moving. The software didn't check for edits during that time and assumed nothing had changed. What kind of error is this?
choices: A race condition
An emergent bias
A truncation error
A false negative
questions.explain: A race condition happens when the order in which concurrent tasks access shared data affects the result. The Therac-25 had two: command-screen editing and a counter that rolled over from 255 to 0.

questions.q: Why does Quinn conclude the Therac-25 team was morally responsible for the harm?
choices: They built the device that caused the harm and were negligent
They held the role of hospital administrators
They deliberately intended to harm the patients
They were convicted of a crime in a court of law
questions.explain: Moral responsibility requires a causal condition (causing the harm) and a mental condition (intending it, or being careless, reckless or negligent). Negligence is enough, so intent is not required.

questions.q: In the May 7, 2016 Tesla Autopilot crash that killed Joshua Brown, why did the system fail to brake for the truck?
choices: A hacker remotely disabled the car's brakes
A race condition in the software's braking module
Brown had switched Autopilot off moments before
The white, tall trailer looked like an overhead sign to radar
questions.explain: The trailer was white and hard to see, and its height gave it a radar signature like an overhead sign. Autopilot had been on for 37 minutes, Brown's hands were on the wheel for only 25 seconds, he got 7 warnings, and the car was going 74 mph in a 65 mph zone.

questions.q: What is the 'hand-off problem' in partially automated driving?
choices: Rideshare passengers refuse to take the wheel in emergencies
Bored drivers need 3-7 seconds to take over, but crises unfold faster
Software can't pass data between sensors fast enough to react
Cars hand control to remote operators who lack proper training
questions.explain: Many emergencies happen in less than 3 seconds. This is why Ford, Volvo and Google planned to skip SAE Level 3 and go straight to full automation.

questions.q: Why does Quinn say eliminating false positives in Uber's self-driving test vehicles was risky?
choices: Removing false positives can create worse false negatives
False negatives only cause passenger discomfort
False positives are always completely harmless
Uber's cars had no sensors able to see pedestrians
questions.explain: Braking suddenly for steam, exhaust or litter is a real problem and can get the car rear-ended, but failing to detect a real hazard is far more dangerous.

questions.q: Which decision does Quinn list as contributing to moral responsibility for the Boeing 737 MAX crashes?
choices: Refusing to update the 737 with fuel-efficient engines
Requiring every pilot to complete simulator training
Installing too many redundant angle-of-attack sensors
Relying on a single angle-of-attack sensor to activate MCAS
questions.explain: Boeing wanted fast FAA certification and no simulator training, so it described MCAS as an extension of Speed Trim. It also did not tell pilots about MCAS and let it activate repeatedly with no limit on stabilizer movement.

questions.q: According to Friedman and Nissenbaum, what makes a computer system biased?
choices: It systematically and unfairly denies an opportunity or good
It was designed by a team lacking any diversity
It produces any error at all, however random or rare
It relies on machine learning rather than explicit rules
questions.explain: A biased system can also assign an undesirable outcome on unreasonable or inappropriate grounds. The key words are 'systematically' and 'unfairly'; random errors alone do not make a system biased.

questions.q: A facial recognition system trained on a data set that is more than 80% white and more than 75% male has a 1% error rate on lighter-skinned men and a 35% error rate on darker-skinned women. Which type of bias is this?
choices: Emergent bias
Fairness by unawareness
Preexisting bias
Technical bias
questions.explain: Bias already present in society, carried in by an unrepresentative or historically unjust training set, is preexisting bias.

questions.q: Only so many search results fit on a screen. The first Google result gets a 27.6% click-through rate, the tenth about 2.5%, and fewer than 1% of users go to page two, so the ranking algorithm itself can introduce bias. Which type of bias is this?
choices: Preexisting bias
Emergent bias
Technical bias
Confirmation bias
questions.explain: Technical bias comes from how designers handle the technical limitations of a system, here limited screen space.

questions.q: Microsoft's chatbot Tay, released in 2016, learned from user input. Malicious users fed it hateful language, it began producing slurs, and it was taken offline within 24 hours. Which type of bias is this?
choices: Preexisting bias
Technical bias
Emergent bias
Training-set selection bias
questions.explain: Emergent bias arises while a system is in use. Tay was not biased at release; it became biased through its interactions.

questions.q: Why are automated decision systems deployed in the first place, according to Quinn?
choices: Software never needs updating once it has been deployed
They promise to be fast, cheap, objective and data-driven
They are guaranteed by design to be completely free of bias
Federal law requires all hiring decisions to be automated
questions.explain: People often make poor decisions by misjudging emotion and logic, relying too much on others' opinions, or ignoring information. Quinn's point is that computerized systems can make poor decisions too.

questions.q: What did researchers find when they tested commercial speech recognition systems on recordings of Black and white speakers?
choices: All systems performed equally well
The systems understood Black speakers better
Only one system showed any difference
Every system understood white speakers better
questions.explain: The finding shows machine-learning systems need to be trained on more diverse data. Speech recognition matters because it improves accessibility.

questions.q: What did Quinn's image-recognition examples show about machine-learning systems?
choices: Image systems are immune to bias because pixels are neutral
They amplified gender stereotypes in their training photos
Google Photos labeled every image correctly from launch
Bias appears only in systems that process written text
questions.explain: Training photo collections mostly showed women cooking or shopping and men coaching or shooting, and the systems amplified those preexisting biases. Google Photos mislabeled Black men as 'gorillas' in 2015, and Google responded by disabling visual searches for primates.

questions.q: What does Quinn say about predictive policing?
choices: It has been banned in every major U.S. city
It uses only live video, not historical crime data
Claimed crime drops lack empirical support
It has been proven to remove bias from policing
questions.explain: Predictive policing analyzes past crimes to decide where to send resources. Memphis, Santa Cruz and Los Angeles reported reductions, but researchers found a lack of evidence for them.

questions.q: A lender removes race from its loan-approval model but still uses applicants' 9-digit ZIP codes. Why might the model still discriminate?
choices: ZIP codes are a federally protected trait
Removing race always guarantees fairness
Lenders may not use location data at all
ZIP codes can act as a proxy for race
questions.explain: This is why 'fairness by unawareness', simply leaving out the protected attribute, fails: correlated features can stand in for it. Quinn adds that there may be several mutually incompatible definitions of 'fair'.

questions.q: How does Quinn sum up the challenge of creating unbiased AI systems?
choices: Impossible, so AI should never be used for decisions
Easier said than done; even definitions of 'fair' may conflict
Simple once companies publish their fairness principles
Solved by withholding protected-class information
questions.explain: Training data must represent the general population and avoid historical injustices. Companies such as Microsoft and Google have stated fairness principles, but turning them into practice is hard.

questions.q: How do computer-related careers compare with mature professions such as accounting (CPAs)?
choices: They are as mature as medicine and law
Certification, licensing, and a degree are not required
150 semester hours and a national exam are required
A license is required in every U.S. state
questions.explain: CPAs need a degree, 150+ semester hours, supervised experience, an exam and continuing education. Because computing lacks these, Quinn says practitioners must take more personal responsibility for their ethics.

questions.q: What happened to the path for licensing software engineers as Professional Engineers (passing the FE and PE exams after four years of experience)?
choices: It became mandatory in all 50 states
Only 81 people took the exam in five years, and it ended
It is required for all safety-critical code
It replaced the CPA exam for programmers
questions.explain: The attempt copied the path used in disciplines such as civil engineering, but too few people took it.

questions.q: According to the preamble of the Software Engineering Code of Ethics, which concern is paramount?
choices: Loyalty to the employer
Personal career advancement
Concern for the public interest
Maximizing shareholder value
questions.explain: The Code is organized around eight principles (public, client and employer, product, judgment, management, profession, colleagues and self), with the public interest first.

questions.q: How does Quinn say the Software Engineering Code should be read?
choices: As a set of rules taken from a single ethical theory
As a whole, with judgment, not as a legal checklist
As a mechanical procedure that settles every case
As a checklist where anything not banned is allowed
questions.explain: Just because the Code doesn't forbid something doesn't make it morally acceptable. No mechanical process decides right and wrong, and the Code draws on several ethical theories.

questions.q: Clause 1.03 says to approve software only if you have a well-founded belief it is safe. Under which principle of the Code does it fall?
choices: Public
Product
Self
Management
questions.explain: Clauses numbered 1.xx belong to the 'Public' principle, acting consistently with the public interest. 'Product' (3.xx) covers quality standards.

questions.q: A manager tells a developer that he will be reassigned to a dead-end project if he keeps raising ethical concerns about the product. Which clause of the Code is the manager violating?
choices: 3.11: Ensure adequate documentation is produced
8.01: Stay current with developments in the field
5.12: Don't punish anyone for raising ethical concerns
2.02: Don't use software obtained illegally
questions.explain: Clause 5.12 falls under the 'Management' principle and protects people who raise ethical concerns.

questions.q: Prof. Singh gives Robert Lone Wolf free advice and recommends a top-ranked LAN security package. She doesn't mention that she has a financial interest in the company that makes it, or that another package was rated a 'best buy'. What does Quinn conclude?
choices: She did nothing wrong, since her advice was free
She should have refused to give any advice
She broke the law and should be prosecuted
She should have disclosed her conflict of interest
questions.explain: Clauses 1.06, 4.05 and 6.05 point to deception and an undisclosed conflict, while 1.08 and 6.02 credit her for volunteering her expertise.

questions.q: System administrator Van Nguyen, who is not authorized to open other people's files, opens a coworker's suspicious-looking files while installing software and finds child pornography. What does Quinn conclude?
choices: He erred in opening them, but must now report discreetly
He acted rightly and should post the evidence publicly
He should delete the files and tell no one about them
He should confront the coworker and demand answers
questions.explain: Van was wrong to violate company policy, but once he knows, he is obliged to tell company authorities. Clause 5.10 reminds him the files might have been planted, so discretion and due process matter.

questions.q: Jean, who works in Acme's support organization, secretly develops a training course at home and takes paid vacation to teach it for East Dakota, competing with Acme's own training. She tells no one at Acme. What does Quinn conclude?
choices: She acted wrongly by hiding a conflict of interest
She was right, since she improved her own skills
She did nothing wrong, since she used her own time
She was wrong only because she broke a law
questions.explain: Clauses 4.05, 2.08 and 6.05 weigh against her, even though 3.04 and 8.04 work in her favor. Acme is likely to question her loyalty, so her actions were wrong and unwise.

questions.q: A team lead replaces 'chairman' with 'chair', uses 'they' for a person whose gender is unknown, and says 'person without housing' instead of 'homeless person'. What is she practicing?
choices: Microtargeting
Fairness by unawareness
Self-censorship
Inclusive language
questions.explain: Quinn's guidance on inclusive language includes person-first wording, gender-neutral pronouns, avoiding stereotyped terms and using people's own pronouns.

questions.q: Which engineer documented the dangers of launching the Challenger at low temperatures, shared the information with the presidential commission, and then faced retaliation from his employer?
choices: Eric Butler of Firesheep
Robert Morris of Cornell
Ruth Goodearl of Hughes Aircraft
Roger Boisjoly of Morton Thiokol
questions.explain: Boisjoly took medical leave, quit, and found consulting work two years later. Goodearl reported defective chips at Hughes Aircraft and later won a False Claims Act suit.

questions.q: Which of Richard DeGeorge's questions for whistle-blowing are the first three, the ones some people treat as enough to make whistle-blowing morally required?
choices: Documented evidence? Will it work? Will you keep your job?
Will media cover it? Do coworkers agree? Has harm occurred?
Serious public harm? Told your manager? Tried every inside channel?
Is it legal? Is it profitable? Is it popular with coworkers?
questions.explain: DeGeorge himself says all five conditions must be met; the last two are documented evidence and confidence it will work. Others say the first three are enough, and still others say whistle-blowing is never required.

questions.q: How does the view of 'whistle-blowing as organizational failure' respond to whistle-blowing?
choices: Organizations should improve communication to prevent it
Harm should be handled by lawsuits after the fact
Whistle-blowing is always a strict moral duty
Whistle-blowers are disloyal and should be punished
questions.explain: On this view whistle-blowing harms both the organization and the whistle-blower, though critics ask whether better communication is realistic. Robert Spitzer argues organizations should return to principle-based decisions. The 'disloyal' framing belongs to the corporate response view.

questions.q: How is moral responsibility different from role, causal and legal responsibility, according to Quinn?
choices: It is not exclusive, so a whole team can share it
It applies only when some law has been broken
It is exclusive and rests with the most senior person
It can be borne by a corporation but not by individuals
questions.explain: Moral responsibility must be borne by people and is not exclusive, unlike role, causal and legal responsibility. Michael McFarland argues a team should be held to a higher standard than any one member, which matters for software built by teams.

questions.q: Between 1979 and 2023, while the U.S. population grew 48%, what happened to manufacturing employment?
choices: It fell 90% as most factories closed
It rose 48%, keeping pace with population
It fell 42%, from 19.4 to 11.2 million jobs
It stayed roughly constant at 19 million
questions.explain: Office jobs have been affected too, including clerical workers, bookkeepers and middle managers.

questions.q: How can automation create jobs, according to Quinn?
choices: Lower prices raise demand and real incomes, creating jobs
Consumer demand stops mattering to employers
Higher prices raise profits, so companies hire more
Governments are forced to hire every displaced worker
questions.explain: Lower prices increase demand for the product, and higher real incomes increase demand for other products. Automation also creates jobs designing, building and servicing automated devices. Quinn notes that widespread unemployment has not occurred in the countries that use automation most.

questions.q: How does Quinn say modern societies have used higher productivity, compared with medieval or ancient times?
choices: To eliminate nearly all manual labor
To cut the standard work week in half
To return to small-scale farming
To raise the material standard of living
questions.explain: Medieval and ancient laborers worked less when wages rose because they weren't consumers. Productivity has more than doubled since World War II, but the standard work week has stayed roughly the same.

questions.q: Stuart cancels a one-week trip to see his parents in San Diego when his boss promises him three weeks' vacation next year and airfare to Australia. An analysis scores San Diego 1 x 1 x 2 x 100% = 2 and Australia 3 x 1 x 1 x 25% = 0.75, and concludes Stuart decided wrongly. Which Bentham factors does it use?
choices: Duration, purity, propinquity, and certainty
Duration, extent, fecundity, and intensity
Intensity, fecundity, extent, and purity
Certainty, extent, intensity, and propinquity
questions.explain: Australia lasts three times longer (duration), the two are equal on purity, San Diego is sooner (propinquity), and San Diego is certain while Australia is only about 25% likely (certainty).

questions.q: In the canceled vacation case, which analysis concludes Stuart did nothing wrong because he broke no promises, deceived no one, and was not obligated to visit his parents?
choices: Virtue ethics and act utilitarianism
Act utilitarianism and rule utilitarianism
Kantianism and social contract theory
Rule utilitarianism and virtue ethics
questions.explain: Kantianism and social contract theory find no broken duties or violated rights. Virtue ethics says Stuart lacked courage and consideration for himself, his coworkers and his parents.

questions.q: Where was the term 'artificial intelligence' coined?
choices: At a 1969 symposium at MIT
At a 1956 workshop at Dartmouth College
At a 1948 conference at Bell Labs
At a 1973 seminar at Xerox PARC
questions.explain: Early AI focused on programming high-level reasoning and problem solving. BASIC was also developed at Dartmouth, which can cause confusion.

questions.q: Which of these early AI milestones is correctly matched?
choices: MYCIN identified unknown organic molecules (1960s)
Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov at chess (1997)
DENDRAL diagnosed bacterial infections (1970s)
Chinook won the Jeopardy! challenge (2011)
questions.explain: DENDRAL identified organic molecules, MYCIN diagnosed bacterial infections, Chinook played checkers (1995), and Watson won Jeopardy! (2011).

questions.q: Why did AI research pivot to artificial neural networks?
choices: Rule-based reasoning fell short at learning; networks can be trained
Neural networks need no training data to improve their performance
Neural networks were cheaper to build than other approaches in the 1950s
Governments banned symbolic AI research after early failures
questions.explain: Neural networks went nowhere in the 1950s because computers were too slow. Results came in the 1980s, such as Bell Labs' handwritten digit recognizer, and later with deep learning.

questions.q: What does 'hallucination' mean for generative AI like ChatGPT?
choices: The system becoming conscious
The system refusing to answer
An attack that corrupts training data
Output that is false or off-topic
questions.explain: ChatGPT, released in November 2022, reached 100 million users in two months. Quinn stresses that it has no true understanding or consciousness.

questions.q: An AI ethics guideline says people should know when AI is being used, the system should be able to explain its behavior, and its actions should be auditable. Which of the five common AI principles is this?
choices: Transparency
Justice, fairness, and equity
Reliability, safety, and security
Responsibility and accountability
questions.explain: Transparency covers disclosure, explainability and auditability. 'Responsibility and accountability' means humans control AI and bear liability for it.

questions.q: How has information technology changed the structure of organizations?
choices: It has required many more layers of middle management
It has made them more rigid and hierarchical than before
Cheap interaction has flattened them and cut out middlemen
It has had no measurable effect on how firms are organized
questions.explain: When communication was expensive, information flowed up and down a hierarchy. Cheap, fast interaction lets information flow flexibly, which supports flatter, more dynamic organizations.

questions.q: What does the evidence Quinn cites show about employee monitoring?
choices: It has no measurable effect on workers
It is illegal at most U.S. companies
It raises focus but lowers job satisfaction
It raises both focus and job satisfaction
questions.explain: About two-thirds of companies monitor employees' Internet use. Monitoring can catch misuse of company resources and illegal activity.

questions.q: How does Quinn define globalization, and what made it possible?
choices: Moving all manufacturing to China, made possible by tariffs
A worldwide network of businesses and markets, enabled by cheap IT
A single world government, made possible by the United Nations
Replacing national currencies with global cryptocurrencies
questions.explain: Falling computing and communication costs made global enterprises feasible by the mid-1990s.

questions.q: Which of these is an argument against globalization that Quinn presents?
choices: It increases unrest and instability
It hurts workers in poorer countries too
It keeps poorer countries from prospering
It reduces competition among firms
questions.explain: Quinn's example is individual Mexican corn farmers who cannot compete with subsidized U.S. agribusiness. Critics also say globalization forces American workers to compete with poorly paid workers and speeds the loss of jobs. The other three options reverse pro-globalization arguments: it increases competition, is a proven route to prosperity, and reduces unrest.

questions.q: What did MIT's 2022 win at the International Collegiate Programming Contest show?
choices: U.S. teams win the contest nearly every year
China has never placed in the contest
It was the first U.S. win in 25 years
The contest is open only to U.S. universities
questions.explain: The contest has been dominated by teams from Russia and China. Quinn uses it as evidence of truly global competition in IT talent.

questions.q: What is the digital divide?
choices: The pay gap between CEOs and production workers
The split between open and closed platforms
The gap between people with and without access to IT
The gap between hardware and software engineers
questions.explain: The underlying assumption is that people with access have opportunities denied to those without. The idea became popular with the World Wide Web.

questions.q: A new technology is adopted first by the wealthiest group, then the middle group, then the poorest. Eventually all three groups use it equally. Which model of technological diffusion is this?
choices: The stratification model
The winner-take-all model
The trickle-up model
The normalization model
questions.explain: In the normalization model, adoption evens out over time. In the stratification model, the order of adoption is the same, but the poorer groups' use stays permanently lower.

questions.q: Which of these is part of Mark Warschauer's critique of the term 'digital divide'?
choices: Access to IT has no effect on opportunity
It wrongly makes the gap a simple matter of access
The term is too technical for the public
The divide has already closed around the world
questions.explain: Warschauer says people fall along a continuum rather than into 'haves' and 'have nots', that it is unclear whether lack of access causes disadvantage or the reverse, and that the Internet is not the pinnacle of IT development.

questions.q: In Quinn's data on Internet access around the world, which region has the lowest share of people with access?
choices: Asia (about 67%)
Africa (about 44%)
Latin America and the Caribbean (about 80%)
The Middle East (about 77%)
questions.explain: Access is higher in wealthier, more literate, English-speaking regions with good infrastructure. North America is highest, at about 93%.

questions.q: What is the debate over net neutrality about?
choices: Whether governments may censor political content
Whether ISPs may charge more for priority routing
Whether software can be patented in the U.S.
Whether ISPs must keep stored email for 180 days
questions.explain: Net neutrality would require all packets to be treated the same. Supporters of tiered service point to services like voice over IP, while opponents such as Google say it would hurt start-ups and innovation.

questions.q: How did U.S. net neutrality policy change between 2015 and 2017?
choices: Repealed by the FCC in 2015, then restored by Congress in 2017
Adopted by the FCC in 2015, then repealed by the FCC in 2017
Established by a Supreme Court ruling in 2015
Required by federal statute continuously since 1996
questions.explain: The FCC issued the Open Internet Order in February 2015 under President Obama and repealed it in December 2017 under President Trump, after which some states introduced their own legislation. India (2018) and the EU (2015) adopted net neutrality rules.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the causes of 'winner-take-all' markets that Quinn identifies?
choices: Stricter antitrust enforcement
Progressive tax structures
Network economies
Salary caps in pro sports
questions.explain: Other causes are IT and efficient transportation, the dominance of English and changing business norms. In a winner-take-all market, a few top performers get a disproportionate share of the rewards. Progressive taxes and salary caps are among the remedies Quinn suggests.

questions.q: In the 2021-22 PGA season, golfers with nearly identical statistics earned vastly different amounts: about $562,000 per tournament for Scottie Scheffler versus about $11,600 for Sung Kang. Similarly, CEO pay rose from about 40 times a production worker's pay in 1980 to about 670 times in 2022. What phenomenon do these examples show?
choices: The winner-take-all effect
The stratification model
The digital divide
Emergent bias
questions.explain: Small differences in performance lead to huge differences in reward. Remedies include cooperative agreements such as salary caps, limits on store hours, progressive taxes and campaign finance reform.
